articles.title_orig: Berkshire Hathaway accelerates stock buybacks, operating profit falls
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Hathaway accelerates stock buybacks, operating profit falls
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.
The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That's more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company's total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.
The sharp increase came as Berkshire's operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.
Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire's railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.
The company's overall earnings, which include Berkshire's sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.
Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.
Berkshire's five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola .
Berkshire's cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate's cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.
— CNBC's Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.title_zh: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who's won?
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests, on 5.
New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon addressed supporters in Auckland as votes were being counted
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests.
New Zealand election 2026: What you need to know
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens â who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops â saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins speaking to supporters
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices â for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.title_orig: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
articles.title_zh: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
articles.content_orig:
Missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media that Russia used 36 missiles to target critical infrastructure. Only four missiles were taken down, Zelenskyy said, highlighting a shortage of interceptors . He also said 172 drones were used in the attacks, which struck Kyiv and 12 other regions.
The president accused Russia of intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and the country's infrastructure ahead of trilateral talks .
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration , the most recent having been in Geneva in February.
Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.
"Russia has a very particular view of diplomacy – as a subtype of aggression," Zelenskyy wrote.
"We hope that the United States, like our other partners, will act on principle," he added.
The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages , national and city authorities said.
Zelenskyy said a kindergarten was "partially destroyed." Photos show rubble near the damaged building.
Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit.
"The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It's very hard. No sleep, no peace — nothing. The children aren't sleeping, and neither are we," she told The Associated Press. "I'm old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?"
Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 892-yard-long Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River. Russia's Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine's armed forces.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city's heating and water supply systems."
Ukraine's Energy Ministry said Saturday's missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.
The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.
Russia also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.
Zelenskyy said that at one energy facility, preliminary findings show Russia used KN-23 missiles "manufactured and supplied by North Korea." He called the use of the alleged North Korean missile "further proof that global sanctions regimes need to be significantly strengthened." Technical assessments at other sites are ongoing.
Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.
Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers.
"She went to get humanitarian aid, and a 3-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?" he said. "She didn't come home, and they didn't find her body there. She isn't in the morgue, and she isn't here alive."
The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia's Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.
The head of Russia's southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged "civilian infrastructure" and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.
The head of Russia's Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.
Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol's Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.

articles.title_orig: A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
articles.title_zh: A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
articles.content_orig:
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.
The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.
"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen , a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."
The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.
"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.
Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.
"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.
Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).
So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).
The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.
"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence .
Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.
In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.
The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.
"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz , a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."
Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.
It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.
There could be other reasons for why the study failed.
"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal , a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.
"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron , a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.
The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.
Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.
It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.
Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.
"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson , a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."

articles.title_orig: Millions of ladders recalled nationwide after numerous reports of head injuries, skull fractures
articles.title_zh: Millions of ladders recalled nationwide after numerous reports of head injuries, skull fractures
articles.content_orig:
Apothecary Pharma recalls compounded tirzepatide vials distributed nationwide due to sterility concerns. Ashley Webster reports on the FDA classification of the recall and the North Carolina company's production practices.
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) is recalling more than 3.6 million Little Giant ladders after receiving dozens of reports of injuries, including head trauma and skull fractures.
The ladders, according to the recall , have a mechanism called "Rapid Locks" that are designed to be inserted into the ladders' rungs to help adjust the height.
According to a statement from Little Giant, the Rapid Locks can fail to become fully engaged, causing the ladders to retract and posing a potential fall hazard to consumers.
The company has received 25 reports of the ladders retracting, 19 of which resulted in injury.
NEARLY 6 MILLION COFFEE MAKERS SOLD AT MAJOR RETAILERS RECALLED OVER BURN RISK
Recalled Little Giant Adjustable Fortress 2.0 ladder (Unknown)
Those incidents resulted in three reports of head injuries which, according to the recall, include traumatic brain injury, skull fractures, concussions, vision loss, hearing loss and cognitive impairment.
The company has also received 16 reports of other injuries such as joint or bone fractures, lacerations and bruising.
Overall, the company has received 39 reports of the Rapid Locks not working properly.
WALMART RECALLS 4.4 MILLION GRILL BRUSHES OVER SERIOUS INJURY RISK
Recalled Little Giant Conquest 2.0 ladder (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission / Unknown)
The recall involves 11 makes of Little Giant's ladders and over 130 models ranging from $100 to $1,000.
Little Giant is adding supplemental warning labels to affected ladders, instructing users to visually verify that all Rapid Locks are fully engaged before climbing.
"You should stop using your ladder until you have received and applied the warning labels included in the repair kit according to the enclosed instructions, which contain further guidance on safely operating the Rapid Locks and maintaining the Rapid Locks with lubrication," Little Giant said in a statement announcing the recall.
The company is also sending repair kits to all known users with Rapid Locks malfunctions.
"The repair kit contains instructions, also accessible via the QR code on the ladder, for safely operating the Rapid Locks and maintaining the Rapid Locks with lubrication," the company added.
Recalled Little Giant Quantum ladder (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission / Unknown)
CPSC advised consumers to maintain the Little Giant ladders' Rapid Locks with lubrication and to evaluate their ladders on a regular basis.
"If a lock does not function properly after this evaluation, the company will offer the choice of a replacement ladder of the same or equivalent model or a refund ranging from a depreciated value determined by date of purchase up to full purchase price for ladders purchased within the past 12 months," CPSC said in the recall.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay's ex-President Peña faces prosecutors after impeachment, house arrest
articles.title_zh: Paraguay's ex-President Peña faces prosecutors after impeachment, house arrest
articles.content_orig:
Santiago Peña’s links to Ueno Bank scrutinized after crisis led to his house arrest and froze millions of bank accounts
Pedro Volpe had just woken up last Tuesday when he saw a message from a friend asking whether his bank account was down, too.
It was a day after payday, and Volpe, 50, a writer and lawyer, opened his banking app and panicked: he could not even see his balance.
Volpe was among nearly 3 million Paraguayans, about 60% of the country’s adult population, whose accounts had been frozen overnight. All were customers of Ueno Bank, a digital lender that aggressively expanded across the South American country in recent years, and which, on Monday night, the central bank ordered into resolution over insolvency.
Ueno is at the centre of a political and economic crisis that has brought Paraguay’s banking system to the brink of collapse. On Friday, it led to the impeachment and house arrest of the rightwing president, Santiago Peña.
Peña had resigned the day before in a vain attempt to retain the special jurisdiction afforded to former presidents – who, under the constitution, become senators for life. Lawmakers stripped him of the seat anyway, meaning Peña will face criminal proceedings in the ordinary courts.
In just a few days, he went from being a market favourite among Latin American presidents and one of Donald Trump’s key allies in the region to facing fierce mass protests, being voted out and placed under house arrest.
The now former president is the subject of an investigation by the public prosecutor’s office over alleged favouritism towards Ueno, which, in just a few years since Peña took office in 2023, went from an obscure digital lender to the bank of choice for most Paraguayans.
“It was very easy to use and to open an account,” said Volpe, recalling that everything could be done quickly on a mobile phone. The bank also offered far more generous investment returns than its competitors did.
“Now I’m having to work miracles to pay my bills,” added Volpe. “A lot of people can’t even afford basic everyday things like food; luckily, I still had some money saved elsewhere, but that has only got me this far. I don’t know what I’ll do next week.”
Ueno was so popular – sponsoring the national football team, the league and the country’s biggest football clubs – and served such a large share of the population that businesses have already reported an overall fall in sales of up to 80% this week. Media outlets belonging to the same financial group as the bank had their operations suspended, including radio stations and the century-old newspaper La Tribuna .
The impact on ordinary Paraguayans was perhaps even wider reaching. The media freeze saw 300 workers having their salaries suspended, initially for 90 days. About 32,000 pensioners whose public pension funds had been invested in the bank were left without payments.
“A lot of people are also not working because they can’t get paid or make payments,” said the historian and political analyst Fabián Chamorro. “Meanwhile, the protests were growing every day, and Peña’s impeachment was the way congress found to prevent a popular explosion.”
A former finance minister and ex-employee of the central bank and the International Monetary Fund, Peña was elected by promising to restore a “great Paraguay” and attract foreign investment.
Soon after taking office at age 44 as the youngest president in Paraguay’s democratic history, he appointed Carlos Carvallo Spalding, who had until then been Ueno’s CEO, to lead the central bank. Less than three months later, Spalding authorised Ueno, then a finance company, to become a digital bank.
Peña himself had about $1m in shares he bought in 2019 in a company that would become Ueno Holding in 2022, the parent company of the conglomerate that controlled Ueno Bank. Even after becoming president, he only disposed of the shares in April 2025. He said he had bought them purely as an “investor”.
“During Peña’s administration, Ueno began receiving various benefits, and the government relaxed the rules to allow public funds to be invested in the bank,” said Chamorro. An estimated $800m to $860m in state and pension funds were invested in Ueno.
A series of internal central bank reports pointing to irregularities – including loans to companies within the same group – were revealed by local media in recent months, but Peña dismissed them as a “false media campaign” against his government.
With the bank having less than half the solvency required to meet its obligations, the central bank ordered it into resolution only after mounting pressure from other banks and opposition lawmakers.
Spalding resigned and, like Peña, was ordered arrested on Friday night. During the week, police had already arrested eight senior executives and directors of Ueno and its controlling group on suspicion of concealing the bank’s deteriorating financial position for months.
The public prosecutor’s office is investigating Peña on suspicion of illicit enrichment, money laundering and influence peddling. He denies all the allegations, and his lawyers said there is no evidence he directed the allocation of pension funds to the bank.
Meanwhile, most affected people still have no access to their own money.
A guarantee fund covers deposits of up to $38,000, which would apply to more than 90% of individual account holders. On Friday, the central bank began making payments to customers with up to $1,565, no outstanding debts and an existing account at another institution.
Paola Benítez, a 25-year-old chef from the capital, Asunción, met all three requirements, but by late Friday afternoon had not yet recovered the money she had been saving for her wedding.
“This has made me a bit anxious, a bit desperate too, because honestly, who am I supposed to go to and ask about this? It’s very strange, very confusing, very sad,” she said.

articles.title_orig: From high-flying AI stocks to tariff-hit alcohol companies, the midterms shook up Wall Street
articles.title_zh: From high-flying AI stocks to tariff-hit alcohol companies, the midterms shook up Wall Street
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks plunged on Thursday as AI and chip stocks sold off, erasing the gains from Wednesday's post-election rally.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) tumbled 3.4%, or more than 1,800 points. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 4.3%, and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 5.5%, with the tech-heavy index closing in correction territory.
The Nasdaq-100 ( ^NDX ) fell 6.3%, erasing $2.3 trillion in market value.
The PHLX Semiconductor index ( ^SOX ) plummeted 12% as Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), and other chip names sank. Wall Street unloaded this year's AI winners , while large-cap tech stocks saw the worst day since the COVID-19 pandemic sell-off.
Investors continued to process the Democrats' sweeping victory on Tuesday and its implications for markets and the economy . Amid relief that election uncertainty has been removed, the stock market continues to sort out the perceived winners and losers of a regime change on Capitol Hill.
Oil prices rose amid uncertainty that President Trump would pursue a deal with Iran to end the war in the Middle East. Optimism grew overnight after Vice President JD Vance said, "The reason we lost [the midterm elections] is the war," in a post on X suggesting the party should push for a resolution to the conflict. Brent crude oil ( BZ=F ) prices traded around $98 per barrel, while US benchmark WTI crude ( CL=F ) stood at $90 per barrel.
A report from Challenger, Gray & Christmas showed layoff plans in October fell to the lowest level since 2023 as companies turned their attention to retaining existing employees, setting the scene for Friday's key employment report.
On the earnings calendar, Duke Energy ( DUK ), Airbnb ( ABNB ), and Lumentum ( LITE ), among others, report results.
Stocks plunged on Thursday amid carnage in the AI trade on Wall Street.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) dropped more than 1,800 points, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) plunged 4.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) fell 5.5%, closing in correction territory.
Chip stocks took the brunt of the beating, with severe losses for Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), and AMD ( AMD ), among others. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) sank 12%.
Institutional investors dumped the top performers of 2026 to lock in gains. Retail traders followed suit, unloading $265 million of equities in their biggest selling day since 2020.
Meanwhile, regulatory concerns weighed on AI data center build-out stocks. SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) also plummeted over fears of regulatory hurdles following Democrats' congressional victory.
Retail investors are dumping US stocks at a pace not seen since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, breaking with their typical market-down-day habit of "buying the dip."
Everyday investors sold a net $358 million in individual US stocks on Thursday as of 2:58 p.m. ET, according to Vanda Research, putting them on track for their biggest single-day net selling spree since March 17, 2020, when retail investors pulled $502 million from individual stocks.
"This is what we would call a total capitulation by retail investors," Viraj Patel, global macro strategist at Vanda Research, said in emailed comments.
The selling marks a departure from retail investors' tendency to scoop up shares when markets tumble. Vanda said there were "no signs of buying the dip" in individual stocks, though some investors continued purchasing leveraged exchange-traded funds such as the ProShares UltraPro QQQ ( TQQQ ) and Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares ( SOXL ).
Patel added that the retreat echoed a broader "buyers' strike" among institutional investors alongside forced selling by systematic and leveraged investment strategies.
The AI trade's marquee stocks got clobbered on Thursday, sparking warnings on Wall Street of an institutional shakeout as investors move to lock in gains.
"They're shooting the generals," wrote Nomura cross-asset strategist Charlie McElligott on Thursday.
The unwinding of the 2026 popular thematic stocks has been "wildly acute" for more than a month, the strategist noted. The primary catalyst isn't about a sudden deterioration in fundamentals, but a frantic dash by hedge funds to lock in their profits before the end of the year.
"Single-name stock moves are absolutely BONKERS," wrote McElligott. "The Momentum/High Sharpe unwind has been so substantial that we are approaching the dreaded 'Round Trip' levels in some trades."
The carnage has hit semiconductor and hardware stocks particularly hard. Shares of Lam Research ( LRCX ) are down 36% over the past month. Applied Materials ( AMAT ) has shed 30% over the past month, while AMD ( AMD ) and Nvidia ( NVDA ) are also down 22% and 15%, respectively, over the same period.
Goldman Sachs ( GS ) promoted 109 employees to its coveted partnership on Thursday, its largest class since 2010, as the Wall Street giant elevated record numbers of asset managers and engineers to its senior ranks.
The new class is nearly 15% larger than in 2024 when Goldman named 95 partners, according to a statement from the bank.
Of the 109 new partners, 60 work in Goldman's investment banking and trading division, while 33 are in Asset & Wealth Management. The firm also promoted 13 engineers.
In a departure from previous years, a Goldman executive declined to disclose the gender and racial makeup of the new class, citing changes in the legal environment. The executive added that with the latest round of promotions, the firm has more than 100 female partners.
Partnership status at Goldman is considered highly exclusive. The firm promotes new partners every two years. The promotion comes with higher compensation and additional financial benefits, including opportunities to invest in the firm's private funds.
Once promotions take effect in January, Goldman will have a little over 500 partners, an executive said, amounting to roughly 1% of Goldman's workforce.
It's a bad day for the stock market.
Major indexes are falling Thursday, with technology stocks leading the sell-off and semiconductor shares among the biggest decliners.
But one rough session doesn't necessarily amount to what investors deem a correction.
A correction generally refers to a decline of at least 10% from a recent high in a stock, index, or other asset. It is typically seen as a meaningful pullback, but one that stops short of a bear market, which is commonly defined as a drop of 20% or more.
That distinction matters after Wednesday's sharp rally. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) and the narrower Nasdaq-100 are each on pace to close Thursday in correction territory, as is the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ).
Meanwhile, the Dow and S&P 500 (down 3% and 4% from yesterday) aren't close to correction territory.
The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) just fell below its 200-day moving average, according to AlphaSpace data (see chart below).
Several individual names, such as Nvidia ( NVDA ), also broke through their 200-day averages, a technical indicator that tracks a stock's long-term trend.
"I think this has been brewing for quite some so much time because there have been so many investors poking at this perceived AI bubble, almost hoping it's going to burst, Hennion & Walsh chief investment officer Kevin Mahn told Yahoo Finance's Market Hang.
"So this type of volatility shouldn't necessarily come as a surprise to anybody … but there's going to be more choppiness ahead," Mahn added.

articles.title_orig: An Update On A Possible ‘GTA 6’ PC Release Date Plans, Due To AI
articles.title_zh: An Update On A Possible ‘GTA 6’ PC Release Date Plans, Due To AI
articles.content_orig:
Yesterday, when reporting on emerging efforts to pipe the console version of GTA VI through a PC’s DLSS-powered Nvidia GPU , we mentioned in passing that PC players could instead just wait for the AI-assisted decompilation port that will no doubt be coming in short order. Now, a former Rockstar tech director says he thinks that exact threat could cause the developer to work faster on the official PC version of its soon-to-release crime/lifestyle simulator.
Obbe Vermeij hasn’t worked at Rockstar since 2009 , but in a new interview with Rock Paper Shotgun , he recalled how artists for the PC version of the original top-down Grand Theft Auto were incensed when the console version squashed the game’s 256-color textures down to 16 colors for the PS1 release.
“So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console,” Vermeij said. “So in those days, it was like PC first and then console second, even though that didn’t really make much sense for the sales, because the PlayStation versions sold way better.”
Those sales caused Rockstar to pivot hard toward the console side of the business, with oft-delayed PC ports of its major games only hitting many months or even many years after their console counterparts. It’s a trend that Rockstar has stuck with even as many formerly console-focused game publishers have started treating the PC as an equally relevant platform and as the line between PCs and consoles itself has gotten much fuzzier in recent years.
The rise of AI-powered reverse-engineering tools —which can quickly turn a console game binary into easy-to-port raw code with incredible brute-force efficiency and minimal human effort—might change that kind of “PC can wait” calculus for Rockstar. “I think I would be concerned, if I was Rockstar, that somebody would just take the PS5 version and get AI to change it to PC,” Vermeij told Rock Paper Shotgun.
To be sure, decompiling a game as complex as Grand Theft Auto VI wouldn’t be as simple as, say, the previous human-led decompilations of early 3D GTA games . But even if an AI coding harness has some difficulty capturing all the details of GTA VI ‘s advanced weather systems and scripted sweat simulations , that doesn’t mean it’s impossible.
Vermeij speculated that reverse-engineering the console version of GTA VI could cost “tens of thousands of dollars in tokens,” and a resulting port probably “won’t be as good as [Rockstar’s] effort” in the end. That said, Vermeij said it would probably be good enough to satisfy some potential PC players and that he “wouldn’t be surprised if there was an effort to get [the releases] a little bit closer together” to get ahead of that.
“What was the case before is that there’s so much effort in developing the game, that it is not possible to rip it off, and that’s completely changed now,” Vermeij said. “So, yeah, we’re going to have to see in the next couple of years how that’s going to pan out.”
While there hasn’t been an official timing announcement for the PC port of Grand Theft Auto VI , reports suggest Rockstar is currently aiming for the first quarter of 2027.

articles.title_orig: Jim Cramer sends a strong signal to Nvidia stock investors
articles.title_zh: Jim Cramer sends a strong signal to Nvidia stock investors
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Chip stocks had their worst day since March 2020 on Thursday, and Nvidia fell 9.26% to $181.60 before bouncing 2.78% to $186.64 on Friday.
A retiree who bought 1,000 shares at $121.79 in June 2024 is still up $64,850, but has given back $52,600 since the Oct. 6 record.
Selling 300 shares would cut Nvidia from 23.7% to 16.6% of a $786,640 portfolio for about $2,918 in federal tax.
Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)
Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shareholders just lived through the roughest week for chip stocks in more than five years. On Thursday, the PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 12.25%, its biggest one-day drop since March 2020, as investors weighed what the new Congress could mean for data center construction. Nvidia fell 9.26% that day to $181.60. On Friday it bounced 2.78% to close at $186.64.
Even after the bounce, Nvidia ended the week 8.8% lower and sits 22% below its record close of $239.24 on Oct. 6.
Take a 64-year-old retiree who bought 1,000 shares on June 10, 2024, the day Nvidia's 10-for-1 split took effect, at $121.79 a share. That was a $121,790 investment. At the October record the shares were worth $239,240. On Friday they were worth $186,640. They also hold $600,000 in other retirement savings and collect $2,500 a month from Social Security, so Nvidia is now 23.7% of a $786,640 portfolio. The question this weekend is whether Thursday was a warning to sell.
The sell-off hit almost every chip name at once. The iShares Semiconductor ETF fell 12.15%, its worst day since March 2020, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF fell 11.21%. Micron fell 17.46% and Lam Research 16.36%. Nvidia's 9.26% drop was one of the smaller ones.
Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.
That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. It covers what your retirement could actually cost, which income sources are worth using, and the withdrawal math that decides whether the money lasts. It is free today from Fisher Investments. Read More Here ›
That gap matters. The stocks that fell hardest sell equipment and memory, which depend on what chipmakers and data center owners plan to spend next year. Nvidia sells into demand that exists today. Investors were pricing in a slowdown in future spending more than a drop in current orders.
Friday brought some relief. Chip stocks rebounded across the board, and Nvidia traded as high as $194.90 during the day before settling at $186.64.
Measured from the purchase, the investment is still well ahead. The 1,000 shares cost $121,790 and are worth $186,640, a gain of $64,850, or 53.2%, in under two and a half years.
Measured from the peak, the shares have given back $52,600 in a month. Thursday alone took $18,530, and Friday returned $5,040 of it.
Nvidia also pays more than it used to. It raised its quarterly dividend to 25 cents a share this year, from 1 cent. On 1,000 shares that is $1,000 a year, a yield of 0.54% at Friday's price. The dividend is small next to the price swings, but it is a sign the company is generating more cash than it needs.
The business is still growing at a pace few large companies have ever matched. Nvidia's revenue over the past four reported quarters reached $302.97 billion, and its latest quarter's revenue was up 105.9% from a year earlier.
The stock is also cheaper than it looks after a run like this. At $186.64, Nvidia trades at about 23.6 times its earnings over the past year. Of the 62 analysts tracked, 59 rate it a buy or strong buy, and their average price target is $327.14, about 75% above Friday's close.
The next real test is close. Nvidia reports its quarterly results later this month, and that report will show whether customers are still ordering at the pace they were.
The risk for this retiree is concentration. Nvidia is 23.7% of everything they own, and at the October peak it was 28.5%. A stock that can fall 9% in a day can fall 30% over a few months. A 30% drop from here would cost about $55,992, almost two years of the $30,000 a year Social Security pays them.
Well-known skeptics are still betting against the sector. Michael Burry disclosed this week that he took profits on a quarter of his bet against the VanEck Semiconductor ETF after Thursday's plunge, and said the rest of the position remains very large.
Selling part of the position is a reasonable option. If the retiree sells 300 of the 1,000 shares at Friday's price:
Taxable gain: $19,455, since each share cost $121.79
Federal tax at the 15% long-term rate: about $2,918
What remains: 700 shares worth $130,648, or 16.6% of the portfolio
If the shares sit in a traditional IRA, the sale itself creates no tax bill today.
Trimming keeps most of the upside if the analysts are right and the next report is strong. It also moves some of a paper gain into cash before the report, when the stock is likely to swing again.
No one knows whether Thursday was the start of a longer slide or a sharp one-day scare. The analyst targets were mostly set before this week. And the $2,918 tax figure assumes the retiree's income keeps them in the 15% long-term capital gains bracket; a larger sale could push part of the gain higher.
A 64-year-old who turned $121,790 into $186,640 with Nvidia is still well ahead, even after losing $18,530 on the chip sector's worst day since 2020. The bigger question is whether 23.7% of a retirement should ride on one stock heading into its next earnings report. Selling 300 shares would cut that to 16.6% for about $2,918 in tax and keep 700 shares in the game.

articles.title_orig: BioWare Lives On: Here Are All The Post-BioWare Projects Currently In Production
articles.title_zh: BioWare Lives On: Here Are All The Post-BioWare Projects Currently In Production
articles.content_orig:
International TV Co-Editor
EXCLUSIVE: The final days of legendary video games studio BioWare will be told in a doc from Shane Fennessey and Adam Scorgie for Canada ‘s Super Channel .
Massive Effect: The BioWare Story will document how the Edmonton, Canada-based games company grew from being founded in 1995 by three medical doctors – Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk and Augustine Yip – to selling 100 million copies of its role-playing games, which include Mass Effect , Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic , Dragon Age and Baldur’s Gate .
Written and directed by Akash Sherman ( Clara ) and co-produced by Canada’s Fennessey Films and Score G Productions , the film has a unique insight into the story, with filming beginning two years before Electronic Arts announced the closure of BioWare on October 21 last month and continuing to lens throughout.
This allowed the filmmakers to capture BioWare’s finale chapter, as the news of the studio’s closure reverberated through the gaming industry. EA decided to shutter studio, which was known for its complex narratives and world building, after recent releases underperformed, and 400 jobs were cut.
Muzyka, Zeschuk and Yip will feature in the film, along with a plethora of major players from the video game world. These include Douglas Reilly, Vice President of Lucasfilm Games; John Riccitiello, former CEO of Electronic Arts; Casey Hudson, game director of Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Mass Effect ; Geoff Keighley, creator of The Game Awards; Victor Lucas, creator of The Electric Playground ; voice actor Jennifer Hale; and longtime BioWare developers Mark Darrah, David Gaider, Drew Karpyshyn, Aaryn Flynn, Mac Walters, Trent Oster, James Ohlen and Caroline Livingstone.
“When the production team asked for our blessing to tell the BioWare story, we were honored and genuinely moved,” said BioWare co-founders Muzyka and Zeschuk in a statement.
“BioWare was never just about the logo or the building. It was about deeply emotionally engaging stories and characters, brought to life by the amazingly talented people on our dev teams, and our excellent production and distribution partners who helped us bring those stories successfully to all corners of the planet, and our passionate fans who defended those worlds, championed them and carried them forward. We’re proud this film honors those who made it all possible. The best stories never really end. They live on in our memories and wait for someone to pick them up again.”
A website has also been set up for the BioWare community to share photos, videos and how the company touched their lives for the chance to appear in the film. “BioWare’s fans have been part of its journey since the very first game,” said Scorgie. “It’s only right that they help us tell the rest of the story.”
“The BioWare founders are my hometown heroes,” added writer and director Sherman. “It’s a privilege and responsibility to share the journey of underdogs who came together to create deeply beloved storytelling. Their golden era kindled a spark in me and in an entire generation. With the studio’s recent closure, the film is now a profound valediction.”
Canada’s Super Channel commissioned the doc, which is being planned for a major film festival run and a world premiere next year. Jhod Cardinal of Upstream Flix is handling worldwide sales. The Canada Media Fund supported production.
“We are thrilled to bring Massive Effect: The BioWare Story to Canadian audiences,” said Kim Ball, EVP Content & Communications for Super Channel. “As an Edmonton-based company, we’re especially proud to celebrate BioWare’s extraordinary hometown story and the people, creativity and groundbreaking storytelling behind some of the most beloved games of a generation.”
Producers Fennessey Films and Score G are behind the likes of Funny Money: The Dane Cook Story , Dolph: Unbreakable , Inmate #1: The Rise of Danny Trejo , Breaking Olympia , Singhs in the Ring and The Great Ones .

articles.title_orig: Boeing retirees are hit with 400% increase in Medicare Advantage premiums
articles.title_zh: Boeing retirees are hit with 400% increase in Medicare Advantage premiums
articles.content_orig:
Christopher McMahon is thinking about going back to work.
The 65-year-old retired from Boeing in 2022 after over three decades in the company’s Seattle-area offices. But the spiking cost of health insurance has him considering whether to get a part-time job.
McMahon, who lives in Des Moines, is enrolled in an Aetna Medicare Advantage plan sponsored by Boeing for its retirees. He and his wife currently pay premiums totaling around $120 per month. Next year, those premiums will jump to over $630 per month for the couple.
That’s an increase of more than 400%.
“We’re shocked,” he said. “This is just so much more than we thought it would be. This is just awful.”
When people turn 65, they become eligible for Medicare, the public insurance program for older adults. At that point, they can choose to enroll in Medicare Advantage, a private insurance option that’s typically more affordable than traditional Medicare, though it comes with restrictions like prior authorization requirements and limited doctor networks.
Some employers offer group Medicare Advantage plans to workers as a retirement benefit. But retirees of Boeing — one of the biggest employers in Washington — are questioning whether they can afford the benefit that was once practically free.
When Boeing first introduced its Aetna Medicare Advantage plan in 2024, the coverage came with a $0 premium, and it remained $0 through 2025.
At the start of this year, Aetna began charging a $60 monthly premium per enrollee. Next year, monthly premiums will have a dramatic increase to $316 per enrollee. The company doesn’t pay for premiums, meaning retirees have to shoulder the increase on their own.
Before 2024, Boeing offered retirees a Medicare Supplement plan, which is a different type of coverage. According to the company, that plan cost enrollees between $327 and $370 per month.
“To me it’s just outrageous,” said Gayle Hughes, who retired from Boeing in 2020 after working at the company for 33 years.
Boeing retirees don’t have to buy coverage through the company, and there are many Medicare Advantage plans available to people in  Washington with premiums as low as $0 per month, though lower-priced plans come with more restrictions.
But Hughes is reluctant to switch plans, because she doesn’t want to lose access to Aetna’s network of doctors. People who drop Boeing’s plan cannot sign back up in the future.
Hughes and her husband plan to stay on the plan for one more year, with the hope that premiums will come back down afterward.
The premium increases come at a shaky time for the Medicare Advantage market. Over the past few years, insurance companies have shrunk their provider networks, raised out-of-pocket costs and eliminated plans that fail to make money. Health insurance premiums in general are rising rapidly , driven by high medical spending and inflation.
In an email, a Boeing spokesperson attributed next year’s higher premiums to rising healthcare claims and plan costs. Aetna did not respond to a request for comment.
Without any help, retirees are struggling to figure out how to absorb the higher costs.
Gordon Hale enrolled in Boeing’s Medicare Advantage plan in September when he turned 65. The upcoming increase will translate to an extra $3,000 in premiums over the course of a year for just himself. To afford it, he foresees some belt-tightening.
He expects that he’ll have to delay some maintenance on his house, including a roof replacement. Hale had planned to take his daughter on a trip during her spring break next year. “That’s probably a staycation now,” he said.
Medicare Advantage premiums are not the only cost of health insurance for older adults.
Most people over 65 also have to pay a standard premium known as the Part B premium, which is adjusted based on income; many have to pay a separate, income-based premium for drug coverage, too.
For some, the combined cost of premiums have spurred a realization that retirement might be more expensive than they anticipated.
Next year, McMahon, of Des Moines, estimates that he and his wife will have to spend at least $2,000 per month on health coverage, after combining all their premium costs and income-based adjustments.
For extra money, the couple have decided to start withdrawing Social Security payments earlier than they had planned. They’ll be hit with a penalty for doing so. They’re also considering dropping the Boeing Medicare Advantage plan for something cheaper, though it might not come with the same level of coverage.
Most likely, McMahon expects that he’ll have to go back to work in some capacity.
“I’m really terrified that we’re going to run out of money,” he said.
It’s not what he wants. McMahon has been enjoying retirement. He likes to wake up early, make his wife a latte and tackle a different project every day, like doing repairs in his garage or pruning back the roses in his garden.
“I’m not at all bored,” he said. “I really have no interest in going back to work.” But he might not have a choice.
He heard about a new retirement housing facility opening up in Des Moines. He’s considering applying for a job there.

articles.title_orig: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
articles.title_zh: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
articles.content_orig:
Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia , Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said .
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN , Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts , Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
after newsletter promotion
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
articles.content_orig:
Americans were unequivocal at the ballot box this week as they expressed disdain for tech billionaires and mistrust of artificial intelligence. With that backdrop, Anthropic is about to try to go public.
The AI company is gearing up for a potentially historic IPO, likely targeting mid-November for its Nasdaq debut. CNBC reported on Friday that Anthropic investors see the company aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from a target of $2 trillion that had been floated in recent months.
From Wall Street to Main Street, it's becoming a tougher environment for Anthropic. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, and it's down to start November after October marked its worst month since March 2025. Chipmakers and neoclouds, the companies most closely tied to the AI buildout, are getting hit the hardest.
Voters rebuked AI in Tuesday's midterm elections, while sending Democrats to sweeping congressional victories across the country. Candidates who advocated for more stringent AI regulation won handily in states like Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Georgia, which will all now have Democratic governors, and local communities opposed data center-related ballot measures in 40 out of 41 cases .
More than half of voters said AI data centers were a "crucial" or "major factor" in who they supported for Congress, according to an exit poll from NBC News.
"People don't want a data center going near them if it's just going to house AI that's going to help a big tech company profit," Maura Austin, a behavioral scientist at the University of Virginia, told CNBC. "What Anthropic is doing when they're going public with such a high valuation is they're really leaning into that big tech, billionaire kind of caricature. I expect that's not going to go well with the public."
Anthropic has long tried to position itself as a safety-conscious company that takes AI's potential risks and benefits seriously. CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company alongside a handful of researchers who defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
The company's enterprise focus has helped it avoid becoming the public face of AI, leaving that distinction to OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman . But with Anthropic poised to become the first pure-play AI company to hit the public market, minting a number of new billionaires and many more millionaires in the process, a heightened level of scrutiny is coming.
"Being a public company, just that by itself pushes you in the limelight," Reena Aggarwal, a professor of finance at Georgetown University, said in an interview. "And then AI is such a hot-button issue that Anthropic will be in the limelight even more."
Matt Kennedy, a senior IPO market strategist at Renaissance Capital, said that's not necessarily a bad thing for Anthropic.
Public markets force greater transparency, he said, and the company could attract new users through its debut. And since AI has become such a mainstream conversation topic, several private companies are already household names.
"I would say that a public company does not deserve more criticisms than a comparable private company," Kennedy said. "So Anthropic should not be put in a harsher public spotlight than OpenAI just because it's public."
Anthropic declined to comment.
AI backlash accelerated over the summer after a series of high-profile safety and security incidents rattled the public. As concerns mounted, the debate over data centers intensified, while tech's hyperscalers  simultaneously boosted their forecasts for capital expenditures, each reaching into the hundreds of billions of dollars.
Anthropic and OpenAI depend on state-of-the-art data centers to train models and serve customers, and they're trying to build out capacity as quickly as possible to meet demand. Anthropic said in an amended IPO prospectus this week that it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion , "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
Americans grappling with inflation and stubbornly high gas prices have grown worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, a proposed data center in their backyard became the physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy toward AI.
In the risk factors section of its prospectus , Anthropic said opposition to data center development has become more organized across jurisdictions, and that the company's public profile could draw particular scrutiny to projects associated with it.
Nicole Greene, an analyst at Gartner, said she expects that Anthropic's executives have long been prepared to contend with AI backlash, especially given the disruptive nature of the technology.
"There's going to be big emotions," Greene told CNBC. "With big emotions and feelings — fear and excitement — comes heightened scrutiny."
Amodei acknowledged the souring sentiment around AI in a post on X in August. He said it's the result of a "crisis of trust," and that people believe companies, the government and the tech industry are always "cooking up some new way to screw them over."
Rebuilding public confidence is going to be an uphill battle as the company begins providing quarterly financial updates.
The University of Southern California published a survey on Monday that found that 71% of respondents don't trust big tech companies to act in society's best interest "at all" around data center development.
"Once you've lost trust, it's hard to gain it back," Wändi Bruine de Bruin, a professor at the University of Southern California's Schaeffer Institute, said in an interview. "The numbers are not good."

articles.title_orig: Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears
articles.title_zh: Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears
articles.content_orig:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire Hathaway shares roared past the S&P 500 index this week as investors moved money away from slumping tech stocks and moved into what appears to be the relative safety of a traditional conglomerate with relatively little exposure to artificial intelligence amid fears massive spending on data centers won't pay off .
One month ago, Berkshire's widely held B shares were underperforming the S&P by 13.6 percentage points for the year.
With help from three more record-high closes this week, Berkshire is now 5.8 percentage points ahead of the benchmark.
Berkshire more than doubled its share repurchases last quarter to $9.6 billion, while operating earnings declined slightly, the company said on Saturday .
Berkshire was up more than 5% this week while the S&P fell almost 2.7%.
The contrast is even sharper with the Nasdaq Composite , which fell 3.4% on the week.
Thursday's especially heavy tech selling pushed the index down more than 10% below its most recent high in what is commonly referred to as a " correction ," but it did make up some of its lost ground Friday .
Two weeks ago, Berkshire's share prices completely erased all of the roughly 15% drop they suffered in the three months following Warren Buffett's surprise announcement at the 2025 shareholders meeting that he would step down as CEO at the end of that year.
Now they are up 6% from the record high closes they hit the Friday before Buffett's revelation on May 3, 2025.
Berkshire is not completely removed from the convulsions around AI.
Abel told us in early September he sees a " significant opportunity " ahead for Berkshire Hathaway Energy to provide electricity to data centers.
He also expected Berkshire would benefit from its big bet on Google parent Alphabet , saying he and Warren Buffett knew AI was "going to have a significant impact on America and businesses," and " we saw Google as a significant player . "
Now that investment is getting negative reviews this week as the stock slumps along with other companies related to AI.
As of the end of June, Berkshire reported it owned almost 106 million shares of Alphabet, including 28.6 million shares it bought directly from the company in June: $5 billion of its Class A shares (GOOGL) for $351.81 each and another $5 billion of Class C shares (GOOG) for $348.20 each.
They are around $284 per share now.
It bought another $7 billion of Alphabet shares on the open market during the second quarter, adding to the position it started building in last year's third quarter, an investment initiated by Warren Buffett .
Bloomberg suggests that "with cracks in the AI trade starting to show, Berkshire's sudden push [into AI] may appear ill-timed."
On June 30, the position had a market value of $37.8 billion and it was the third largest equity holding in Berkshire's portfolio.
Since then both the Class A and Class C shares have dropped by around 20% and the stake is now valued at $30.2 billion , falling behind Coca-Cola's $38.3 billion to the portfolio's #4 position.
(In just over a week, we'll find out whether Berkshire made any changes to its Alphabet position during the third quarter ending September 30.)
Bloomberg quotes CFRA Research analyst Cathy Seifert as saying, "I do think that part of this may be a conscious decision to increase their exposure. One has to ask the question though, is it a little late?"
But the article notes that "for dedicated value investors and longtime Berkshire observers, such jitters may not really matter," with Keefe Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields saying Abel probably sees bets on AI as a long-term wager on the technology's potential, in keeping with the "conservatism that you would expect at Berkshire Hathaway."
At Barron's , however, Andrew Bary sees what he estimates is a $3 billion loss on Alphabet as part of a "disappointing" long-term trend in Berkshire's stock choices
"The company hasn't created much value from stock picking during the current decade" even though the "S&P 500 has returned 150% since the end of 2019 and tech stocks have quadrupled."
While Berkshire's investments in five Japanese "trading houses ," Chevron , and Chubb have done well, "there have been plenty of losers or simply mediocre investments that have been closed out."
He cites Verizon , HP , Paramount (now Skydance) , General Motors , Constellation Brands , and Pool .
While he estimates Berkshire's Occidental Petroleum investment is up about 20% from what it paid, OXY is "far behind most energy stocks" amid this year's big increase in crude prices.
Bary also lists stocks that have continued to rise in price after Berkshire cut its stakes, with Apple being the worst offender.
That stake has been reduced by 75% since 2023 at what Bary calculates is an average selling price around $200 per share, well below AAPL's current $342.
Despite those sales, Apple is Berkshire's largest equity holding with a market value of $78 billion . The stock is up 1200% since Berkshire started buying it at the beginning of 2016, at a time when many thought the company had already seen its best days.
Bary thinks Abel will probably keep Berkshire's core equity investments but may concentrate more on his strengths going forward: improving Berkshire's operating companies and making new acquisitions.
His conclusion: "Barring a market rout, equity investing may not be central to Berkshire anymore.
"And if any new Berkshire holdings are revealed soon, it may not be a good idea to buy them. The record hasn't been great."
Berkshire Hathaway's disclosure that it had made a relatively small $27 million addition to its $4.1 billion Sirius XM position helped fuel an ongoing rally that lifted the satellite radio company's shares to a 52-week high this week.
On Thursday morning last week, Sirius XM reported a 14% increase in its Q3 free cash flow, 5,000 more self-pay subscribers, and it raised its 2026 full-year financial guidance.
The stock ended 4.9% higher that day at $28.67.
On Friday, Monday, and Tuesday, Berkshire bought more than 924 thousand shares at an average price of $29.10 as the stock continued to gain ground, ending Tuesday at $30.80.
Berkshire disclosed the buys late Tuesday evening, apparently helping to fuel an additional 8.4% gain as the stock closed at $33.40 on Wednesday.
It hit a 52-week intraday high of $33.76 on Thursday but finished lower Friday at $32.40.
Overall, Sirius XM is up 18.6% since the earnings release and has gained 62.0% so far this year.
It's the first addition to Berkshire's stake since late-July and early-August last year.
In 2025, it bought a total of 7.3 million shares at an average price of $21.86.
The position is likely one of portfolio manager Ted Weschler's stocks.
Pacific Power, a unit of Berkshire Hathaway's PacifiCorp, is asking California regulators for a 57% rate increase that would raise the typical residential electric bill by $120 a month.
The Wall Street Journal calls it a "stunning request even in an era of rising electricity costs."
The utility says the hike would be partially offset by a 14% decrease taking effect on January 1.
A lot of the $103 million that would be generated by the increase is already being spent on efforts to make power equipment in the sparsely populated and heavily wooded area more resistant to wildfires.
The utility is facing around $637 million in liability claims for fires in 2020 and 2022.
This week, Reuters reports , Oregon's Supreme Court heard arguments on whether to revive a jury verdict that could expose PacifiCorp "to tens of billions of dollars of potential damages over its role in four Oregon wildfires in 2020."

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.content_orig:
Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.
Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.
Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
Zelensky wrote on Telegram that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".
Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.
"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.
"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."
In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.
The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.
Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.
The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.
She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.
She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.
Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire , which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia , with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.
Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.
He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.
"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."
Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.
Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

articles.title_orig: Governor-Elect of Texas Announces Plans to Control Elon Musk
articles.title_zh: Governor-Elect of Texas Announces Plans to Control Elon Musk
articles.content_orig:
The governor-elect of Texas Gina Hinojosa made it clear on the campaign trail that she would work to rein in data centers and billionaire tech barons. And now that she’s headed into office, that means playing hardball with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
“We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms,” Hinojosa said Thursday in an interview with CNN , as quoted by Bloomberg . “It cannot be just running over the people of Texas, and that’s what changes now that I will be governor.”
A central part of Hinojosa’s campaign was demanding an immediate moratorium on new data center construction until lawmakers have established tighter regulations and stronger protections for local communities.
In the Thursday interview, Hinojosa reiterated her commitment to placing more stringent regulations on data centers by saying she would “balance” it with keeping Texas a business-friendly state.
She also shared that she’s already making moves to crack down on Musk. Amid speculation that Texas officials have been considering a sale of state park land to SpaceX, Hinojosa said she spoke to the head of the Texas Parks & Wildlife Department to “request that no action be taken,” per Bloomberg .
“It is such an important resource,” she told reporters in Austin, hours before the CNN interview.
Wall Street and the AI industry are watching Hinojosa closely, as Texas has become the nucleus of the data center boom. Over a quarter of the US’s planned data center capacity resides in the state.
Musk is deeply invested in the state, having relocated his companies SpaceX and Tesla there from California. He’s also reportedly exploring sites to build another large data center in Texas , to add to the controversial “Colossus” facilities he operates in Greater Memphis. That’s not to mention the quarter of a billion dollars he poured into the midterms to support Republican candidates.
Of course, Musk could simply do what many think is impossible — or at least economically infeasible — and ditch terrestrial AI instrastructure altogether.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote on X , following the brutal election loss.
