articles.title_orig: British soldier ignored order to pull his SIM card, then got blackmailed
articles.title_zh: British soldier ignored order to pull his SIM card, then got blackmailed
articles.content_orig:
An Estonian newspaper recently revealed that a British soldier disobeyed a direct order to remove the SIM card from his cellphone before being deployed to a part of Estonia, approximately 90 miles west of the Russian border.
As a result of his refusal to engage in this element of operational security (opsec), the soldier, Daniel Barton-Kennedy, had his phone hacked, and nude photos of himself were stolen and used as blackmail against him.
Eventually, Barton-Kennedy was court-martialed for disobeying a lawful command, pled guilty, was reduced in rank, and ordered to serve 10 months in detention.
According to a 21-page British appeals court document shared with Ars Technica by Eesti Ekspress, the Estonian newspaper that first reported on this saga, the story begins in January 2026.
At the time, Barton-Kennedy was a corporal, with over seven years of service, serving in the 1st Battalion of the Duke of Lancaster Regiment of the British Army.
His unit was deployed to participate in “Exercise Eastern Warrior” in Tapa, Estonia, roughly halfway between Tallinn, the capital city, and the Estonia-Russia border.
While in the United Kingdom, on January 7, Barton-Kennedy, along with other members of his unit, were briefed on their orders and given specific instructions to “remove SIM cards and switch off location settings and to use a trusted virtual private network on all personal electronic devices.”
Once the unit arrived in Estonia, days later, they were given further briefings and reminders of this policy. Despite this, Barton-Kennedy ignored the instruction.
On January 19, Barton-Kennedy informed his platoon commander that he had received a message “from an unknown party who had acquired nude photographs of him from the photo section of his mobile phone and had identified him on social media.”
Barton-Kennedy initially acquiesced to paying the attacker 100 British pounds ($133) but balked when he was asked to pay 250 British pounds ($333), and only then informed his platoon commander what had happened.
Eventually, Barton-Kennedy was court-martialed and pled guilty at a hearing on July 30.
During that process, according to the court filing, Barton-Kennedy understood the orders that were given to him at the time, but asked the court to “consider the personal circumstances” that he faced at the time. Without his phone, he told the court, he could not reach his daughter on her birthday, nor his pregnant partner.
In a written statement, Barton-Kennedy said he was stunned when he received the first blackmail message.
“Despite still being in a state of shock and uncertainty, I recognised that I had a duty to report the compromise without any further delay,” he wrote.
Additionally, he said that he “deeply regrets” the incident and added that serving in the British Army “has been one of the greatest privileges of my life.”
Barton-Kennedy appealed the sentence, which was denied in August 2026.
In response to an inquiry for comment, Lt. Col. EP Mackie, a British Army spokesperson, told Ars in a statement that the security measures imposed are meant to protect the safety of military personnel.
“Any breaches of Army security measures that might compromise personal safeguarding or operational security will be dealt with swiftly, and offending personnel can expect uncompromising disciplinary action,” he wrote.

articles.title_orig: Schools scramble after Google gives AI ultimatum
articles.title_zh: Schools scramble after Google gives AI ultimatum
articles.content_orig:
Google is rightfully facing blowback for forcing K-12 schools to enable AI if they wanted to keep using Google search. The company quickly backtracked and decoupled and turned off the services by default, but made it clear search will continue to be just another AI chatbot. This mandate forces an ultimatum on educators: accept generative AI or de-google your school.
Students, teachers, and parents across the U.S. are now years into an argument about how schools should respond to the growth of AI-enabled tools. Google decided to skip this debate and take this choice from schools. In August it activated AI chatbot Gemini for 150 million K-12 students on Google Classroom, leaving educators scrambling to respond . A few months later, Google introduced a new way to turn it off — but now administrators would also be turning off Google search .
Google walked this back somewhat, clarifying that Gemini, Gemini notebook, and Search will have their own controls and will be off by default. But because of Google’s broader approach to force AI on all search users, this change is still an example of a tech monopolist pushing unwanted changes into the classroom.
It’s no secret that the biggest companies in AI  are operating at a huge loss , in the hope they can follow Uber’s enshittification playbook . Offer a cheap convenience at a major loss until old systems atrophy, then flip the script to reduce wages and raise consumer costs—whether that’s paying with cash or with data.
This puts Google in the odd position of an incumbent, with around 90% of search traffic . It needs to not only make good on its own AI investment, but protect its dominance from new AI tools. It’s not just enough to offer its own AI mode, it needs to turn search into AI mode, while engaging in clumsy self-preferencing that is eating its own ad revenue .
The problem with this approach is the public is split on AI, to put it mildly. Some users will welcome these changes, but the rest are stuck in an all-or-nothing bargain. Anyone concerned about the accuracy of AI overviews or their impact on click-through rates for online communities and small publishers can just deal with it . The bet is any inconvenience in switching to an alternative is enough to keep you trapped.
Google can and should offer a way to disable AI overviews. Smaller services like DuckDuckGo* and Brave search have simple and persisting AI settings which don’t require login. These services also don't mince words and make a distinction between generated AI summaries, suspected AI results, and the backend use of AI to curate links.
It’s not enough to point to opaque workarounds , either. Adding “-ai” to your Google search will usually remove AI Overview, but so will “-unicorn”. This trick isn’t meant to be an AI off-switch, it’s a quirk of how AI Overview was implemented and can change at any time. These tricks also don’t generalize well to settings for system administrators . Hacks might work for now, but everyone—including administrators—deserve clear set-and-forget controls for the tools they rely on.
De-googling your life isn’t easy, and for schools it can be even more difficult. For decades Google has gone after schools to foster life-long Google users—resulting in many institutions being deeply entrenched in its ecosystem despite data privacy concerns . That’s because schools face major switching costs when moving to a competitor. It takes more than flipping a setting—it means a lengthy contract process, staff retraining, and a cumbersome migration of past work.
The difficulty of switching makes granular controls even more essential, particularly for a hot-button issue like generative AI. Few parents would send their kids to AI-driven schools , but they may want their kids to learn tools like search as they exist outside of the classroom. However, many parents and teachers concerned with AI disrupting learning are pushing major school districts to implement temporary AI moratoriums for young students. These pauses are meant to make sure any introduction of AI fits the needs of students and is done in a way that actually makes sure educators are prepared.
But in either camp, this is a choice that must be made by schools, not Google. Teachers know more about what their students need than a trillion-dollar tech company, and this expertise should be respected in their own classrooms.
Google’s self-preferencing and desperate attempt to eventually recoup on an AI money pit must be tempered with more fine-tune controls over generative AI. It’s in Google’s own interest to stop abusing its dominance to piss off users, advertisers, and school communities. It’s also Google’s responsibility as an adjudicated monopolist.
*DuckDuckGo is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.
An open internet where people can freely build, share, and remix each other's work is a powerful engine of grassroots innovation we’ve all benefited from. articles.title_orig: Thieves walked right past it. Turns out it was the real treasure
articles.title_zh: Thieves walked right past it. Turns out it was the real treasure
articles.content_orig:
Look around your house. Could something ordinary be hiding a big secret? For one Romanian family, the answer was yes.
For decades, an elderly woman used a heavy reddish stone to hold her door open. She had picked it up from a stream near Colți, a village in southeast Romania, People reported. The stone was actually a 7.7-pound chunk of amber worth about $1.1 million.
Amber is tree sap's tougher cousin. It's hardened tree resin that turned into a fossil over a very long time, National Geographic explains. Trees make resin to seal up cuts in their bark.

Thieves once broke into the woman's home. They took gold jewelry but left the heavy rock behind, the science site Futura reported.
After she died in 1991, a relative who inherited the house took a closer look. He sold the stone to the Romanian government. Experts in Poland found it is between 38 million and 70 million years old, ScienceAlert reported. That means it may have formed while dinosaurs still roamed Earth.
The amber is now a national treasure on display at the Buzău County Museum, where it has been since 2022. Its director told the Spanish newspaper El País it is one of the largest pieces of amber in the world.
This kind of amber, called rumanite, is found only in Romania, according to The Times of India . Its deep red, brown and nearly black colors set it apart from the lighter amber found near the Baltic Sea.

articles.title_orig: Inside the Operation That Helped Ukraine Turn the Tables
articles.title_zh: Inside the Operation That Helped Ukraine Turn the Tables
articles.content_orig:
In the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk direction , as we noted in our previous sitrep, the situation has stabilized, and the advance of Russian assault troops around the town of Mykolaivka has effectively come to a halt. This is confirmed by new posts from the pro-Russian Slivochny Kapriz project, featuring geolocated footage of Russian strikes on Ukrainian positions in the villages of Piskunivka , Rai-Oleksandrivka , and Tykhonivka .
In the context of Operation Vivaldi, the 3rd Army Corpsâ use of ground robots equipped with grenade launchers was discussed . Now, footage has emerged showing a large-scale assault involving such robots, apparently in the Lyman direction , judging by the reference to the Russian Armed Forcesâ 3rd Motorized Rifle Division, which is part of the 20th Combined Arms Army. Pro-Russian sources report that 28 robots were destroyed by drones. On the one hand, launching such a large-scale robot assault without cover from friendly drones looks like a mistake. On the other, it may have been used as a diversion while assault infantry approached Russian positions along a different route.
The pro-Russian Slivochny Kapriz project has published its estimate of the Russian Armyâs advance in October, according to which the RuAF captured an additional 7.25 kmÂ² of territory. This is virtually zero compared with September, when the project recorded an advance of 177 kmÂ². We had expected that, if the trend observed in the first half of the month continued, the project would record a net loss of territory for the first time in several years of tracking. We do not know which territorial gains were included in the calculation to produce a positive figure.
Notably, these figures are close to the territorial gains by the AFU reported by Volodymyr Zelenskyy: 10.4 kmÂ² in October. At present, the Russian advance is approaching zero when the territorial gains of both sides are taken into account. Starting in November, the pace of offensive operations is expected to decline further with the onset of colder weather and the loss of foliage.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) reported on its Telegram channel that UAV operators of the Alpha Special Operations Center killed 2,146 Russian soldiers and wounded another 1,052 over the course of a week. This would amount to approximately 300 Russian soldiers killed per day, or more than 9,000 per month if extrapolated. This represents a substantial increase compared Ð° with figures reported in previous months: 6,000 âneutralizedâ in July and August , and 7,600 in September . The SBU claims that this particular unit leads the Ukrainian Defense Forces in the number of enemy targets struck.
Meanwhile, the Unmanned Systems Forces reported that their drones killed approximately 300 Russian soldiers per day in October, which would amount to another roughly 9,000 killed per month. This means that just two formations reportedly account for 18,000 Russian soldiers killed per month.
In our assessment, the RuAF's total irrecoverable losses (those killed in action, permanently disabled personnel, prisoners of war, and deserters) may amount to approximately 25,000-30,000 personnel per month. If the Unmanned Systems Forces and Alpha alone account for 18,000 KIA, less than half of Russia's total irrecoverable losses would be left to account for all other categories of irrecoverable losses and the results of operations by all other Ukrainian military branches, including artillery. If our estimate were incorrect and Russian losses actually reached nearly 50,000 per month, as claimed by various sources, the situation for the RuAF along the frontline would already be critical, as losses would significantly exceed recruitment levels (approximately 30,000 personnel per month). In that scenario, we would expect to see a genuine collapse of the frontline rather than the current situation, in which Ukrainian and Russian territorial advances are roughly comparable.
One argument supporting the credibility of Ukrainian figures on Russian losses is the e-points system and the verification of strikes through the Delta situational awareness system. However, we see no reason to assume that publicly released reports necessarily correspond to the actual statistics of units recorded in the internal system.
Michael Kofman is also skeptical of some Ukrainian public claims. In a podcast with a serviceman from the AFU's 3rd Corps, Kofman asked him not to cite an unrealistic casualty ratio between the two sides.
The Economist has estimated that between 374,000 and 770,000 Russian military personnel have been killed, with total casualties, including the wounded, estimated at between 1.4 million and 2.1 million. Many Russian-language media outlets ran headlines featuring only the upper bound, even though the difference between the upper and lower estimates exceeds the lower estimate itself, making it incorrect to present 770,000 as an established death toll. For comparison, by Oct. 30, BBC News Russian and the independent Russian media outlet Mediazona, together with volunteers, had established the names of 285,023 killed Russian soldiers. If we still assume that open sources account for 45-55% of deaths and that our previous formula works (though we no longer believe this to be the case), the actual number of Russian military personnel killed would be approximately 520,000. Due to high drone activity and an extremely low rate of advance, the recovery of bodies from the gray zone is difficult, and deaths are recorded in obituaries and government registries only after substantial delays. Therefore, a more complete picture of casualties for 2026 will likely emerge only in a year or two. The estimate of "around half a million killed" appears plausible, but the available data do not allow us to confirm or rule out The Economist's upper estimate of 770,000.
The humanitarian operation in occupied Oleshky ended on the evening of Nov. 1. According to the latest figures , about 750 people were evacuated from the town (both sides decided not to disclose the exact number). Most of those who wanted to leave went to Ukraine, traveling by air from Anapa to Gomel and then by bus through Belarus. Some residents chose to go to Russian-controlled territory. Thousands of people remain in the town and its outskirts, so humanitarian missions need to continue.
The General Staff of the AFU and other Ukrainian military officials said Russian forces used the ceasefire to rotate personnel and bring up equipment and munitions. This does not, however, suggest that Russia is preparing an offensive against the city of Kherson : the Dnipro remains a formidable obstacle, and Russian troops cannot supply a large force on the river's right bank. Earlier, Sky News, citing Ukrainian marines, also reported ceasefire violations by the RuAF and published footage purportedly showing the violations. However, Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, did not confirm these allegations.
Yana Lantratova, the Russian Commissioner for Human Rights, said the Russian side is doing everything it can to help citizens and protect their rights. But Russia, as the occupying power, bears direct responsibility for protecting civilians who remain in Oleshky and for meeting their basic needs. Russian authorities could have evacuated residents from the dangerous area near the front line much earlier. The evacuation should continue even after the joint humanitarian operation has ended.
The US State Department has approved the sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles to Ukraine for $2.1 billion, but deliveries are not expected before 2030. To obtain the munitions sooner, Ukrainian officials are proposing that the United States and other partners transfer PAC-3 missiles from existing allied stockpiles and replenish them later with missiles produced under the new contract. Such an exchange is technically feasible, but it requires a political decision by the US administration

articles.title_orig: Bunny ears, nudity and strict rules: What it’s like on a ‘lifestyle’ cruise
articles.title_zh: Bunny ears, nudity and strict rules: What it’s like on a ‘lifestyle’ cruise
articles.content_orig:
When Nicole gets ready for a cruise, her packing list goes beyond the typical swimsuits, sundresses and sandals.
Although she plans to spend much of her time topless and poolside, the 50-year-old mother from Indianapolis has already packed more than one suitcase to bursting for her latest trip.
Nicole, who withheld her last name due to privacy concerns, is preparing to set sail on the Wonderland Cruise , a voyage from Miami to the Caribbean onboard one of the world’s largest cruise ships.
“There’s a different theme every night,” Nicole said. “I have a neon yellow and pink bikini for the Glow Party and some shoes that light up. The first night’s theme is Down the Rabbit Hole for Alice in Wonderland, so I have a leather zip-up dress, leather bunny ears and high red and black boots with a heel for that,” she said.
For a steampunk-themed night, Nicole is bringing maroon lingerie with fishnet stockings and a sexy hat with goggles.
“Fetish Night is super easy because I just have some black lingerie that has chains that kind of hang off of it,” she said.
Clearly, Wonderland isn’t your average cruise.
A full takeover by couples-only charter company Bliss Cruise of Royal Caribbean’s nearly 6,000-passenger Wonder of the Seas is being billed as one of the largest “lifestyle” gatherings ever. The seven-night sailing departs on November 9 from PortMiami.
For those inside the subculture, “the lifestyle” is the preferred shorthand for consensual non-monogamy, encompassing everything from swinging to open relationships.
Why cruise ships are sailing to a phantom destination that doesn’t appear on any map
Nicole, who participates in the lifestyle and cruising with her husband of 27 years, says that meeting up with friends from previous Bliss Cruise sailings and making new ones at sea and in port calls like Curaçao and Aruba will be a key part of the week’s fun.
“We always joke with people and say it’s like the high school reunion that you want to go to,” she said.
For some, lifestyle cruises answer a call of the wild and offer the chance to let loose at sea beyond the usual casino tables, ice skating spectacles, waterslides and snorkeling excursions.
It’s a tourism sector that appears to be growing. While cruise industry organization Cruise Lines International Association did not respond to CNN Travel’s questions about this charter-cruise niche, “lifestyle” cruisers have noted more options on larger ships.
“What we’re seeing today is a not just a growth in the number of (lifestyle cruise) brands, but a significant increase in the size of the boats they occupy,” said Mickey Gordon, who hosts the podcast Casual Swinger . Gordon, who also uses a pseudonym for privacy reasons, said that while lifestyle cruises used to be niche events with 800 or so travelers, today’s ships are some of the largest at sea, easily selling out with 5,000 guests or more at a time.
And the reason these cruises are so popular is simple, Gordon said.
“There is simply nowhere on earth you can go that has more ‘people like me’ than a lifestyle cruise. That fact alone sells the trip,” he said.
The Wonderland Cruise, which has been sold out since March 2026 , says it will welcome 5,802 registered guests, all 21 and older, onboard Wonder of the Seas.
They hail predominantly from the United States, which accounts for 87% of bookings, followed by Canada and other nations. Bliss Cruise said guests from 47 countries will be aboard.
Passengers on the cruise represent a near-even split between male and female guests. It’s a requirement that each cabin has at least one man and one woman. “Throuples,” in this case three people with at least one man and woman among them, are permitted to share a cabin (foursomes with two women and two men, while rare, are also allowed). Just over half of passengers on the Wonderland Cruise are between the ages of 45 and 59, according to the company.
Super-sized cruise ships are becoming the norm. Is there an end in sight?
Cabin rates for bookings made in December 2024 ranged between $1,630 per person for interior cabins and more than $21,000 per person for the Royal Loft Suite.
“We do a full charter of the entire ship. We essentially buy the cruise from the cruise line, and then we market that as a specialized lifestyle cruise charter,” Russell Stephens, the CEO of Bliss Cruise, told CNN Travel.
Despite popular misconceptions about lifestyle events, he said the goal isn’t an uninhibited free-for-all, but rather creating a secure, judgment-free space for open-minded couples.
“I think people can expect a lot of fun, and it’s not what some people would perhaps expect,” said Stephens, who said he is in “the lifestyle.”
“It’s really about providing a sex-positive experience for open-minded people,” he said.
Like many major cruises, Bliss has its own app that registered passengers can access before their vacation to browse the hour-by-hour activities offered each day of the cruise, communicate with other guests who have RSVPed for the same events and create personal pages similar to dating profiles.
Categories like “life Interests” — with options as benign as boating, cars, reading, cooking and parenting — are followed by “sex interests,” including dirty talk, massage and hot wife (“a married or partnered woman who engages in consensual sexual relationships with other people — typically men — with the full knowledge, consent, and often encouragement of her primary partner”), among others that are far more risqué.
The cruise’s app details workshops and seminars, many of which cost an additional fee and are already sold out. These range from relatively tame breathwork courses and speed dating sessions to kink and fetish workshops.
There are multiple daily meet-and-greets at bars and other ship venues, too, for people who fall into categories such as Under 45, Over 45, French, Veterans, Sober & Sexy, Silver & Sexy (seniors) and Hall Pass, which is described in the app as not a pass “to have sex in the hallways,” but rather “permission from your partner to engage in sexual activity without your partner being present.”
Meeting and talks geared toward newbies are also plentiful.
“There are a lot of workshops around just being new to the lifestyle and what that is,” Stephens said. “So we try to cater for people, and we really try to welcome newbies into the lifestyle. It’s sort of like they want to think about it, they’re dipping their toes into it, they’ve kind of had a fantasy or whatever. But maybe they’ve never done anything.
“We don’t want people like deer in the headlights,” when they come onboard, he said.
Bliss Cruise is not the only operator catering to lifestyle voyagers.
Other major players include Desire Cruises , a couples-only option with sailings in the Caribbean, the Mediterranean and Adriatic Seas, Asia and North Africa. LLV Club sells lifestyle cruise itineraries in places like Fiji and Tahiti along with South Korea and Japan. Killing Kittens also offers options on the high seas.
On land, there are hotels aimed at the lifestyle-curious and veterans alike, such as Hedonism II in Jamaica, where the mantra is “Be Wicked for a Week.”
‘The Love Boat’: How a TV show transformed the cruise industry
Lifestyle vacations attract a wide cross-section of society, Stephens said. Desire passengers who were interviewed by CNN Travel agreed.
“We’ve met CEOs, we’ve met housewives, we’ve met people in real estate, people who work for the National Security Agency, lots of lawyers and doctors, hotel owners, a math teacher and crazy rich Asians,” said Alice, a physician from the New York City area who has been on two Desire cruises with her husband Bob, a doctor. (The couple spoke under pseudonyms to protect their privacy.)
Alice and Bob are in their early 50s and have been married for 29 years. They first dipped their toes in at a lifestyle resort in the Caribbean in 2019 and are booked on their third Desire cruise, from Lisbon to Morocco, in 2027.

articles.title_orig: A new group of senators from both parties will vote on how to save Social Security. Here’s what they’ve said about it
articles.title_zh: A new group of senators from both parties will vote on how to save Social Security. Here’s what they’ve said about it
articles.content_orig:
Democrats rode a blue wave of Senate pickups on Tuesday, flipping seven seats in red states and winning control of the chamber , while Republicans will also see some fresh faces. Together, the 17 newcomers from both parties will join the next Congress in taking on one of Washington’s most-dodged problems: how to keep Social Security paying full benefits.
The program’s trust fund is projected to run dry in late 2032 . After that, payroll tax revenue would cover only about 78% of scheduled benefits—forcing an automatic cut of roughly 22% unless Congress acts.
Senators elected to full terms this week serve until January 2033, so the deadline falls on their watch. And because Social Security can’t be changed through budget reconciliation, a fix will likely need 60 votes and support from both parties.
Nearly all the newcomers addressed Social Security during their campaigns. As Fortune previously reported , the issue isn’t quite the third rail it used to be, but “protecting” the program can mean very different things.
Here’s what each incoming senator has actually said they would do.
Juliana Stratton, D-Illinois — Stratton said she would eliminate the cap on wages subject to the payroll tax, according to The Times Weekly . Social Security payroll taxes now apply only to the first $184,500 of a worker’s yearly earnings. Eliminating that cap starting in 2027, without increasing benefits for the additional earnings taxed, would close an estimated 58% of Social Security’s projected 75-year funding shortfall, according to the Social Security Administration’s actuaries .
Josh Turek, D-Iowa — Turek said he would lift the $184,500 cap and opposes raising the age for full benefits.
Adam Hamilton, D-Kansas — Hamilton would raise the earnings cap rather than eliminate it , arguing that someone earning $1 million shouldn’t pay the same Social Security tax as someone earning $184,500. He didn’t take a firm position on the retirement age.
Andy Barr, R-Kentucky — Barr opposed changes for people already retired and called for bipartisan reforms for younger generations. He didn’t name specific tax or benefit changes but said reforms should encourage more private and employer-sponsored retirement savings.
Troy Jackson, D-Maine — In a September Bangor Daily News op-ed , Jackson called for scrapping the payroll tax cap and increasing benefits, while ruling out privatization and raising the retirement age.
Abdul El-Sayed, D-Michigan — In his final debate, El-Sayed said the payroll tax cap should be removed and that Social Security benefits shouldn’t be taxed.
Eliminating taxes on benefits without replacing revenue would cost Social Security about $1 trillion over 10 years, plus an additional $700 billion for Medicare, according to a July analysis published by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.
Peggy Flanagan, D-Minnesota — Flanagan backs Sen. Bernie Sanders’ Social Security Expansion Act, Bloomberg Government reported . The bill would apply payroll taxes to wages above $250,000, eventually eliminate the cap, and raise benefits. Her campaign site also supports eliminating taxes on benefits.
Kurt Alme, R-Montana — Alme says savings from cutting waste, fraud, and abuse elsewhere in government should go toward Social Security. In an October debate , he pointed to his experience as Montana’s budget director but didn’t propose changes to the cap or the benefit formula.
Chris Pappas, D-New Hampshire — Pappas opposes raising the retirement age, cutting benefits, and privatization. His campaign highlighted his cosponsorship of the Social Security Fairness Act, the 2025 law that boosted benefits for public workers with outside pensions.
Roy Cooper, D-North Carolina — Cooper made the 2032 deadline a staple of his stump speech. He opposes benefit cuts and says wealthy Americans should contribute more to the program but hasn’t specified how.
Annie Andrews, D-South Carolina — Andrews supports eliminating taxes on Social Security benefits but hasn’t laid out a plan to close the funding gap yet.
James Talarico, D-Texas — Talarico wants to eliminate the payroll tax cap for people earning over $400,000, Texas Public Radio reported .
Barry Moore, R-Alabama — Moore’s Senate campaign website backed cutting taxes on Social Security benefits. He was also an original cosponsor of the Senior Citizens Tax Elimination Act , introduced in February 2025. The bill would remove Social Security benefits from federal taxable income and transfer general funds to replace the revenue the trust funds would lose.
Harriet Hageman, R-Wyoming — Asked how to prevent Social Security cuts during an August 2026 primary debate , Hageman said growing the economy, creating jobs, and getting more people into the workforce would help shore up the program. Like Moore, Hageman was an original cosponsor of the 2025 bill to end federal income taxes on benefits.
Tatiana Sataua is a News Fellow at Fortune covering business, technology, AI, and consumer culture.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s midterm drubbing adds to the populist right’s losses. France’s Le Pen could still win
articles.title_zh: Trump’s midterm drubbing adds to the populist right’s losses. France’s Le Pen could still win
articles.content_orig:
No one in power gets a free pass. HuffPost holds leaders accountable, exposes abuses and uncovers the truth through independent reporting. Help us keep asking the hard questions.
Already a member? Log in to hide these messages.
LONDON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Europe’s far-right politicians have begun to distance themselves from Donald Trump following the Democrats ’ victory in the US midterm elections – but have mostly avoided directly criticising the president himself.
The realignment is notable as many of the leaders celebrated their ideological ties with Trump following his victory in 2024, with some of them visiting Washington DC since then and receiving backing from his billionaire ally Elon Musk.
Jordan Bardella, leader of France’s National Rally, which most polls suggest could form the next government, typified the political shift.
Trump’s second term was less isolationist than his first from 2017 to 2021, Bardella said. “American intervention regarding Iran carries very heavy consequences” for economies around the world, he added, without mentioning Trump as being behind that intervention.
In Germany, Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, also attributed the loss to the Iran war. “Trump had promised his voters not to pursue an interventionist foreign policy ... This broken promise has now come back to haunt the Republicans ,” she told news outlet T-Online.
Trump acknowledged the war with Iran had played a role in his party’s losses but said he stood by his decision.
In Italy, Matteo Salvini, leader of the far-right League party, which is part of the ruling coalition, said, “the American result was influenced above all by the wars, international tensions and the increase in the cost of living, the consequences of which fall directly on families.”
“The hope is that this vote can represent an acceleration towards the end of the conflicts and a return to peace,” he said.
Roberto Vannacci, a former Italian general who leads the far-right Futuro Nazionale party, said the US result showed the political dangers of failing to deliver on electoral promises.
Vannacci has previously expressed admiration for Trump’s “America First” brand of nationalist politics but has since criticised the president over foreign policy.
“Trump failed to live up to expectations, was unable to bring the war between Russia and Ukraine to an end and launched a war against Iran,” Vannacci told ANSA news agency, arguing that the resulting rise in energy prices and economic and stock market turmoil had hurt the US middle class and contributed to the election result.
TIES WITH TRUMP COULD BECOME AN ‘ELECTORAL LIABILITY’
Europe’s far-right leaders were distancing themselves from Trump for obvious political advantage, according to analyst Mujtaba Rahman, managing director of political risk consultancy Eurasia Group. “His growing unpopularity, particularly over the cost of living, risks turning what was once a political asset into an electoral liability,” he told Reuters.
Rahman said far-right leaders appeared to want it both ways: to reap the “ideological momentum of Trumpism” without being tarred by the “chaos and economic disruption of his presidency”.
“The risk is that Trump and his MAGA allies, who see Europe’s far right as ideological partners in their struggle against the European establishment, could respond by withdrawing their political support or even turning against them,” he added.
One of the few to play down the scale of the Republicans’ defeat was Dan Dungaciu, vice-president of the opposition hard-right Alliance for Uniting Romanians, who argued that reports of Trump’s “political death” were “greatly exaggerated”.
He added, “Donald Trump does not automatically become a powerless president. Instead, he moves from a presidency backed by Republican majorities to one in which the executive and Congress will check each other much more intensely.”
In Spain, the leader of the far-right party Vox, Santiago Abascal, made little attempt to temper his move away from Trump, telling reporters he was “in Spain and not in Michigan”.
“I care quite little about what happens in other places,” said Abascal, who has in the past touted his alliance with Trump and the MAGA movement.
Rupert Lowe, leader of the far-right Restore Britain party, also blamed the decision to attack Iran for the Republicans’ defeat, calling it a “catastrophic mistake.” He added, “What has this war achieved? Absolutely nothing of worth.” Lowe did not, however, include in his lengthy X post the name of the president who launched the war.
The right-wing populist Reform UK leader Nigel Farage acknowledged on Wednesday the election had been a “complete and utter rout” for Republicans, despite his earlier prediction that expectations of a Democratic landslide were overblown.
Farage, who has regularly touted his friendship with the US president and visited the White House last year, told GB News there was now “potential” for a rift between Trump and Vice President JD Vance.
“It turns out many of the young men, those who follow all sorts of right-wing influencers who voted for Trump in 2024, actually voted Democrat yesterday. It was a punishment beating, very much I think, because of the war, the extended war in Iran, and the cost of fuel,” Farage added.

articles.title_orig: This Israeli Vows to Oust Netanyahu. Here’s How.
articles.title_zh: This Israeli Vows to Oust Netanyahu. Here’s How.
articles.content_orig:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog must decide who gets the first attempt at forming a government, after an inconclusive election left both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, short of a parliamentary majority.
Herzog has said he will task a candidate with forming a government on Sunday. Eisenkot has received the endorsement of a majority of lawmakers – but only thanks to parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, which won a record 19 seats in October’s election, but whom Eisenkot has ruled out bringing into government.
During consultations between party heads and Herzog , which ended on Thursday, 67 out of 120 Knesset members endorsed Eisenkot, while only 46 endorsed Netanyahu.
Netanyahu’s endorsements fell seven short of his bloc’s 53 seats after United Torah Judaism, one of his longtime allies, withheld endorsements over his coalition’s failure to exempt ultra-Orthodox Israelis from military service.
Herzog has not publicly committed to either side, saying that while the numbers may look clear, “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” made it hard to tell who could build a coalition.
Prior to the October 27 elections, reports emerged that the president wanted to push for a national unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s rival parties to avoid another election.
No bloc has secured the 61 seats needed to form a majority government. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious alliance has 53, four Jewish-led parties backing Eisenkot hold 48, and the Arab-led parties hold 19.
Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.
United Torah Judaism has signalled that its support was available for the right price, but Shas endorsed Netanyahu on Wednesday.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, would need to lure an opposition party to his side. A unity government with the two men rotating as prime minister – and excluding Arab-led parties from government – is another option, but many Netanyahu rivals have ruled out serving under him.
So far, it seems unlikely that they will.
The Arab-led parties are the Joint List, an alliance of three parties, and the United Arab List (Ra’am). They hold 11 and eight seats, respectively.
Ra’am says it is willing to join an Eisenkot-led government, while the Joint List has ruled out joining but offered to help put him in office from the outside.
Both endorsed Eisenkot during consultations with President Herzog, but he has refused to bring either into government unless they meet certain conditions, including recognising Hamas as a “terrorist organisation”.
Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas, whose party joined an anti-Netanyahu coalition in 2021 and became the first party representing Palestinians to enter government in Israel, has expressed support for disarming Hamas, but declined to label it as a “terror” group.
However, Israeli law allows Eisenkot to become prime minister with fewer than 61 seats if his proposed government wins a parliamentary confidence vote – which the two could help him secure.
Eisenkot could form a minority government in the meantime and later secure a majority by luring the two ultra-Orthodox parties by making concessions on the conscription issue.
In positions that many observers see as highlighting the second-class nature of Palestinian citizens in Israel, some of Eisenkot’s allies have opposed any reliance on Palestinian lawmakers, while Netanyahu’s Likud has threatened that cooperating with the Arab-led parties would be “dangerous to Israel”.
Senior Joint List member Ahmad Tibi told The Associated Press that rejecting a partnership would prove Israel is “an ethnocracy, not an absolute democracy for all citizens”.
First, an end to Netanyahu’s rule.
The Joint List said its unanimous backing for Eisenkot answered a “public demand” to stop Netanyahu and his government returning to power.
By widening Eisenkot’s lead, it said, it hoped to narrow the path to a unity government that keeps Netanyahu in office. Its support, it added, did not mean dropping its reservations about an opposition that had not shown readiness to confront Netanyahu’s approach or incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel.
In return for outside support, Arab-led parties are seeking guarantees for Palestinian citizens, including an end to house demolitions and incitement, action against crime, and a political horizon for Palestinians.
Tibi told The AP he had no illusions that this would end Israel’s wars or bring a Palestinian state, but said a “repair government” would improve Palestinian citizens’ lives, including, potentially, by tackling violent crime in their communities.
Ra’am leader Abbas has also said ending the government of Netanyahu, and far-right figures such as Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, is a priority.
The nominee chosen by Herzog will have 28 days to form a coalition, extendable by 14 more. If they fail, another nominee will be chosen and granted 28 days.
If the second nominee fails, a parliament majority can back a third candidate, and be granted a final 14 days.
If once again no government is formed, the Knesset will be dissolved and an entirely new election called within 90 days. This would mean Netanyahu staying on as caretaker prime minister.
Nehru Jamhour, an analyst of Israeli affairs, told Al Jazeera that this drawn-out impasse was the likeliest outcome, and Netanyahu’s preferred one. He said that Netanyahu was hoping that a repeat election could weaken his rivals and depress turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.

articles.title_orig: Top Gulf official offers glimmer of hope on Trump-Iran nuclear talks as threat of war hangs over region
articles.title_zh: Top Gulf official offers glimmer of hope on Trump-Iran nuclear talks as threat of war hangs over region
articles.content_orig:
Reporting from Dubai, Fox News Digital examines how the UAE is balancing hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough with preparations for escalation, as Emirati officials and experts warn of Iran's threats to regional security and the global economy.
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — A senior United Arab Emirates official says he is cautiously optimistic about negotiations between the United States and Iran, citing progress through Qatari mediation over the past days, even as fears of renewed military confrontation continue to grip the Middle East .
"We see some progress. … We hope that both sides will be able to reach a point where they will start building trust and engaging in a way to avoid the war, to find a political solution. … I am a little bit optimistic, but I don't exclude the other option," Dr. Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee of the UAE's Federal National Council, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.
His remarks came as Reuters reported on Nov. 5 that Iran had submitted a new nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar. Tehran, however, continued to insist that the U.S. meet seven conditions before negotiations could proceed, including sanctions relief and an end to the American naval blockade.
IS THIS TRUMP’S LAST ‘LAST CHANCE’? CEASELESS STRING OF BROKEN CEASEFIRES FUELS DOUBT OVER IRAN DEAL
Dr. Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the UAE Federal National Council's Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee, speaks to Fox News Digital in Abu Dhabi about the Iranian threat, regional security and prospects for diplomacy. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
President Donald Trump has not ruled out further military operations, while Iran has threatened broader retaliation if fighting resumes.
For the UAE, which endured thousands of Iranian missile and drone attacks earlier this year, the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough offers hope. But its leaders are making clear that hope cannot replace preparedness.
"We plan for the worst. We hope for the best. … We always make sure that we are ready to deal with all the challenges or the threats," Al Nuaimi said.
That combination of optimism and caution was evident during Fox News Digital's reporting trip across the Emirates, where daily life appeared remarkably normal despite the uncertainty surrounding the country.
On an evening in downtown Dubai, restaurant terraces were packed, tourists filled the streets and crowds gathered around a fountain show set to music that moved between Arabic songs and Western pop hits.
Businesses were operating, international visitors were arriving and the city continued to project an image of prosperity and openness.
IRAN’S STRAIT OF HORMUZ SCHEME COULD DERAIL ONE GULF NATION’S BRIGHT FUTURE
Crowds gather to enjoy an evening fountain show in downtown Dubai, United Arab Emirates, as daily life continues despite the threat of renewed regional conflict with Iran. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
The contrast was just as striking in Abu Dhabi, where Fox News Digital attended the opening of ADIPEC 2026 , one of the world's largest energy conferences, against the backdrop of continuing tensions with Iran and the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz.
Days before the conference, ExxonMobil and Chevron executives had canceled their planned appearances because of security concerns, Reuters reported on Oct. 29.
Yet inside the exhibition halls, delegates from around the world gathered to discuss investment, announce partnerships and explore technological solutions to the energy crisis .
It was a demonstration of the UAE's determination to keep its economy moving while preparing for a security environment that has changed dramatically.
TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION
United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan greets President Donald Trump at Abu Dhabi International Airport on Thursday, May 15, 2025. (AP Photo/Altaf Qadri)
The UAE has already paid a significant price for its proximity to the conflict.
More than 3,000 Iranian missiles and drones targeted the Emirates during the war, according to figures cited by The Associated Press on Nov. 2. The attacks caused casualties and damage to civilian infrastructure.Although no new Iranian attacks had targeted the UAE since May, the threat of renewed confrontation has kept the country on alert.
Al Nuaimi emphasized that while the UAE considers itself a nation committed to peace, it will not hesitate to protect its population.
"Every nation, when it is attacked, [has] the right to defend their people, their sovereignty, their nation," he said.
But he also drew a clear distinction between the Iranian regime and the Iranian people, who are repressed by the regime. "The Iranian people deserve to be respected, accepted. They have great values, great civilization, and they are our neighbor."
MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT
A man walks past a housing compound as a tall plume of black smoke ascends following an explosion in the Fujairah industrial zone on March 3, 2026. Iran's strikes on Gulf neighbours since February 28, following the US-Israeli attack, forced the UAE to shut its airspace, blindsiding travellers who thought they were headed to one of the region's safest holiday destinations. (Fadel SENNA / AFP via Getty Images)
Despite the confrontation with Iran, Al Nuaimi rejected the suggestion that the UAE's relationship with Washington should be judged primarily through the current conflict or any particular U.S. administration.
"We don't see our relationship with the United States through these conflicts, through security and defense. No, it's a partnership. It's a strategic partnership. It is a sustainable partnership. … Our main partnership is with the United States as a nation, with the American people."
He emphasized that the relationship extends across education, medicine, technology, energy and investment, and is intended to endure political changes in Washington.
"We don't look at the United States through a certain administration. Our engagement and partnership with the United States ... [is] with the nation. It's with the people. ... We have the flexibility and the ability to [adapt] and engage with any administration."
The comments come at a sensitive time for Gulf governments, whose security relationships with Washington have become more consequential as Iran threatens regional infrastructure and international shipping.
At ADIPEC's opening ceremony on Nov. 2, Dr. Sultan Al Jaber, the UAE's minister of industry and advanced technology and chief executive of state-owned energy giant ADNOC, emphasized that the country's ability to withstand the crisis was the result of years of preparation. "We did not write our resilience playbook during this disruption. We wrote it years before," Al Jaber told the audience.
The message was consistent with what officials and analysts repeatedly emphasized during Fox News Digital's visit: the UAE intends to remain a reliable international partner despite the possibility of another regional escalation.
GULF COUNTRIES STRONGLY CONDEMN IRAN'S DRONE ATTACK ON BAHRAIN AS RISING TENSIONS THREATEN MOU
The exhibition floor at ADIPEC 2026 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, where global energy companies showcased new technologies and innovations amid growing concerns over energy security and regional instability. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
In a separate exclusive interview with Fox News Digital in Dubai, Mohammed Baharoon, director general of the Emirati research center B'huth, argued that the confrontation with Iran has fundamentally expanded the meaning of national security.
"Our resilience now becomes our deterrence," Baharoon said.
The UAE's security strategy, he explained, involves far more than intercepting missiles and drones. It also means ensuring reliable energy supplie

articles.title_orig: Parents sue Google after discovering what daughter was doing with AI on school Chromebook
articles.title_zh: Parents sue Google after discovering what daughter was doing with AI on school Chromebook
articles.content_orig:
Tech companies have spent years telling parents they're working to make their products safer for children. But ongoing jury trials, settlements and related litigation against the likes of Meta , Google and Snap suggest that they're not doing enough.
The latest examples landed this week. Snap confidentially settled a case claiming that its technology caused severe psychological distress to two teenage users. Meta , TikTok and YouTube previously settled with the plaintiffs in the same suit. And Google was sued this week by the parents of a child who allegedly suffered a psychological crisis after chatting with the Gemini AI chatbot in Google Classroom.
Concern is intensifying as artificial intelligence companies pursue trillion-dollar valuations, and established internet giants pour money into developing advanced AI models while pushing them into the classroom. Products and features intended to maximize engagement can have detrimental effects on users, thus warranting "broader systemic changes in tech design, particularly when children are using them," said developmental psychologist Kate Blocker.
"I think it's so so important that children's safety is being considered when these products — AI, social media, et cetera — are being designed, and not after the fact as these problems emerge," said Blocker, the director of research and programs for the nonprofit Children and Screens.
Snap's settlement this week, which spared CEO Evan Spiegel from testifying in a Los Angeles court, continues a general trend of tech companies attempting to shield themselves from public scrutiny due to the various high-profile child-safety related trials this year, said Joseph McNally, the director of emerging litigation at McNicholas & McNicholas.
The case was one of several lawsuits related to the social media personal injury trial that Meta and YouTube lost earlier this year. More trials are slated to commence in March.
"I view this settlement and the other settlements in this space as an effort by tech companies to turn a corner, not only because I think that there were real legal challenges, but also the reputation of their products, the reputation of their companies has really been hit," said McNally, a former acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California.
"The parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner," a Snap spokesperson said in a statement.
"We've built safeguards, launched safety tutorials, and partnered with experts and because safety is never finished, we remain committed to continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community," the Snap spokesperson said.
But there remains a federal case involving Meta, TikTok, Snap and YouTube and a litany of nationwide school districts, along with various state attorneys general suits . In August, Meta agreed to pay nearly $17 billion to settle with a group of state AGs in a child mental health case. Some AGs are still pursuing similar suits against Meta's rivals.
The social media lawsuits have helped inform parents and the public about how the industry designs products used by teenagers and children, McNally said.
"It's the technology arms race that continues," he said. "What is oftentimes missing is how you balance that participation in the arms race with utility and then product safety."
Google ran into more criticism this week for moving too fast. The New York Times reported on Tuesday  that K-12 schools that don't allow use of Google's AI tools for students will lose access to search. Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the Times that, "Search and AI are deeply integrated."
That coincided with the new lawsuit against Google centering on a teen's alleged suicidal crisis that the parents attributed to the company's Gemini AI. The plaintiff's attorneys allege that "despite Gemini's known risks, Google hastily integrated" Gemini into Chromebook computers for school children.
"We are reviewing the claims in the lawsuit and we take this very seriously," a Google spokesperson said in a statement. "We've worked extensively with medical professionals and academic experts to build features that help young people find critical support and trusted resources when they need it."
Google and its internet peers have for decades been able to rely on Section 230 .
Passed in 1996, the federal legislation has protected social media companies from being sued over content posted by their users. That's why plaintiffs' attorneys and state AGs have been focused on alleged harms stemming from the design of the tech platforms as opposed to their content.
Some plaintiffs are using the same tactics against AI companies. OpenAI faces several lawsuits from state AGs and plaintiff attorneys, taking cues from the social media suits in alleging that the design of ChatGPT can pose risks to children.
The litigation could become a growing financial risk as the company plans for a potential blockbuster IPO. OpenAI competitor Anthropic, which is planning to go public this month, highlighted the issue in its prospectus , even though the Claude creator prohibits children from using its product.
"This is a clear indication that tech companies anticipate more litigation risks than they did a decade ago," said Michele Neitz, a professor at the University of San Francisco School of Law.
Blocker said that the highly personalized nature of current AI-powered chat apps makes it "a little bit unpredictable" to determine exactly what the apps will say to kids. She stressed the importance of testing and evaluating these products for children's developmental safety from the start, "not after harms start happening."
This collective litigation has helped educate the public on the potential pitfalls of poor product design choices, Blocker said. And it could be a catalyzing force for change in the tech industry.
"Certainly there's a hope that this will motivate real systemic change, both from a regulation standpoint and internal company decision-making standpoint," Blocker said.
If you are having suicidal thoughts or are in distress, contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 for support and assistance from a trained counselor.

articles.title_orig: How Democrats used anger over data centers to flip red states
articles.title_zh: How Democrats used anger over data centers to flip red states
articles.content_orig:
As the dust settled on Election Night, Democratic operatives working to elect James Talarico were surprised by the breadth of his victory across Texas’ 254 counties. But even then, one area stood out.
Kaufman County, southeast of Dallas, is the site of two massive data center projects that have sparked local backlash. The largest city in the county, Forney, is already working to outlaw new data centers within its city limits.
The solidly red county was one of 55 counties where a pro-Talarico super PAC, Lone Star Rising PAC, targeted voters within 5 miles of a proposed or approved data center project. The PAC sent them a series of mail pieces and digital ads blaming the project on the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton.
“WARNING,” one of the mailers read, addressing the voters by their first names and adding, “There is an existing or proposed data center near you in Kaufman County. Ken Paxton made it easier to build.”
Talarico carried Kaufman County by 1 percentage point as he notched a striking 12-point victory statewide, helping lead Democrats to statewide victory in Texas for the first time since 1994.
It was one of many examples where backlash to data centers fueled Democrats’ staggering victories in the midterms. From statewide races to local ballot initiatives, voters demonstrated sweeping support for a tougher stance toward data centers, if not outright opposition to their continued development.
About a quarter of voters said AI and data centers were “crucial” to their vote in the midterms, trailing higher priorities such as the cost of living and corruption, according to CNN’s Voter Poll. But when voters were asked about building data centers in their communities, they were overwhelmingly opposed by a roughly 3-to-1 margin.
“It was overwhelming, unequivocal, bipartisan backlash from the bottom up that was showing up in every corner of my district,” said Michigan Rep.-elect Will Lawrence, who flipped a Republican-held House seat after centering his campaign early on opposition to data centers.
GOP candidates had to contend with President Donald Trump’s strongly supportive stance on data centers. By the final weeks of the election, even Trump seemed to concede the AI industry had political problems when he started proposed rebranding AI as “super intelligence.”
Some Republicans are already warning they need a different strategy on the issue for 2028.
The Alliance for a Better Future, a conservative AI policy group, issued a memo the day after the election arguing that it was “impossible to ignore the strong impact Super Intelligence (SI) policy had on this election and how connected it is to economic concerns in particular.” The memo urged Republicans to “recalibrate” and “course correct” ahead of 2028.
One GOP strategist involved in the midterms said any Republicans who want to be competitive in the next presidential race “needs a better playbook.”
“The economy may have been the top issue of this election, but what people are missing is that AI and data centers drove a lot of that angst,” said one GOP strategist involved in the midterms. “AI will likely move to the top of the issue grid in 2028.”
Lawrence stood out for how early – and aggressively – he staked his campaign on data centers. His first TV ad of the primary opened with him standing in the middle of a field, warning that “tech billionaires want to turn this whole field into a massive data center that will jack up your energy bills and ruin our home values.”
There was hardly a national firestorm over data centers when Lawrence attended a Howell Township planning board meeting in October 2025 to protest a proposed data center. It was one of several such meetings he went to throughout his campaign.
But by the end of the midterms, it was hard to find a race where candidates were not arguing over the issue, racing to keep up with public opinion that cut across party lines.
Democratic candidates generally talked tough on data centers, and some, such as Lawrence, even pushed federal moratoriums on them. Republicans at times echoed calls for new restrictions but also touted their economic benefits and arguing they were necessary to stay ahead of China in the AI race.
Dan Diorio, a top official at the Data Center Coalition, a trade group, argued the industry needs to do a better job of showing Americans how data centers could address their concerns about the cost of living. He argued residents of Loudoun County, Virginia, are seeing tax relief due to the data center boom there, although Virginia politics have also been reshaped by concerns about spiking electricity costs due to data center demand.
“People need to see it and feel it,” he said.
Ohio was one of the biggest battleground states for data centers.
The winner of the Senate race, Democrat Sherrod Brown, branded GOP incumbent Jon Husted as “the face of data centers,” citing his support for data center investments as lieutenant governor. The line of attack was so potent that the National Republican Senatorial Committee issued a memo in August warning that data centers were “the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”
The NRSC did not respond to a request for comment for this story.
Husted sought to neutralize the vulnerability in September by spearheading legislation to combat rising energy costs from data centers. Senate Democrats blocked it .
The battle also played out at the local level. Voters in at least 10 Ohio cities passed charter amendments to ban construction of large data centers, according to the anti-data center group Conserve Ohio. The ballot measure in Granville, which is outside Columbus, received over 80 percent support.
In another red state — South Carolina — Democrat Annie Andrews pulled off a major upset in the Senate after persistently labeling the Republican incumbent, Darline Graham, as “Data Center Darline.” Andrews flipped Colleton County, which voted for Trump by 19 percentage points. It was one of the counties that Andrews visited to speak out against local data center developments.
The issue was a vulnerability for Graham as early as her primary, when she said during a debate that “we have to have data centers.” Her position, which she later moderated, drew attacks from multiple fellow Republicans at the time.
A new super PAC aligned with the data center industry, Building the Future, made a late push for Graham in the general election, spending $2.5 million on her behalf. But that spending fueled further attacks that she was beholden to the industry.
Data centers came up in notable ways in other House races.
Mitchell Berman, the Democrat who defeated Republican Rep. Bryan Steil of Wisconsin, ran an ad that showed him shooting a clay pigeon labeled “Data Center.” And in Arizona’s 1st Congressional District, Democrat Amish Shah prevailed after bluntly saying he did not want any data centers in his district.
Shah’s Republican opponent, Jay Feely, went for a more nuanced position, the kind that some Republicans are now second-guessing after Tuesday’s wipeout.
“We have to win [the AI race], we can’t let China win it,” Feely said in one media appearance , “but at the same time, you have to be able to talk to the person who doesn’t really care about China and this fight we’re in, who cares about their life. And so you have to make the argument about why data centers are necessary.”
In Texas, home to the second most data centers in the country, Talarico was not the only statewide winner who ran on cracking down on data centers. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa went further than Talarico did and called for a moratorium on data centers until the Legislature could pass “real protections.”
“We need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections,” Hinojosa told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Thursday. “We can have a strong economy, strong industry and protections for the people of Texas. Those things are not mutually exclusive.”

articles.title_orig: California's Great America in Santa Clara to close in 2027
articles.title_zh: California's Great America in Santa Clara to close in 2027
articles.content_orig:
California's Great America amusement park in Santa Clara is set to close on Labor Day 2027, the park announced Friday.
The 2027 farewell season for the amusement park ends a decades-long history. The park opened in 1976 as Marriott's Great America. The park has undergone multiple ownership changes over the years. Great America is currently owned and operated by Six Flags.
"For more than five decades, this Santa Clara theme park has brought people together, created family traditions and served as the backdrop for unforgettable memories," Dave Vosejpka, park manager of California's Great America, said in a news release. "The farewell season is an opportunity for generations of Bay Area guests to return, spend time with family and friends, and revisit the attractions and traditions that have made the park in Santa Clara, California, such a meaningful part of the community."
The announcement comes as the park's land lease is set to expire in June 2028 and will not be renewed. Cedar Fair, the park's previous owner, which later merged with Six Flags, sold the Silicon Valley land of the park and has since been leased back.
The park, located next to Levi's Stadium, will begin its farewell season in March and details will be released at a later date regarding operating days and hours.

articles.title_orig: Six Pallets of NVIDIA Hardware Worth $11.4 Million Stolen on the Way to Texas
articles.title_zh: Six Pallets of NVIDIA Hardware Worth $11.4 Million Stolen on the Way to Texas
articles.content_orig:
OAKLAND, Calif. (KGO) -- Authorities are investigating the theft of more than $11 million worth of Nvidia computer hardware in Oakland, in what experts describe as a sophisticated cargo heist targeting one of the world's most valuable technology companies.
According to reporting by the Bay Area News Group, the theft involved $11.4 million worth of Nvidia cargo that disappeared after departing Oakland on its way to Texas.
The shipment, consisting of six pallets of Nvidia hardware, left Oakland on Aug. 29 and was bound for Fort Worth, Texas. Authorities said the cargo was picked up as planned by a truck identified as a food transport company.
Investigators later lost track of the vehicle in San Bernardino County.
In a statement, Oakland police said: "The Oakland Police Department is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026."
Olaf Groth, a professor at UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business and has expertise in artificial intelligence, emerging technology and global economics, said Nvidia chips are highly sought after.
"There's lots and lots of incentives to hijack those chips anywhere where security is weak," Groth said.
He said the chips can command significantly higher prices outside the United States.
"These chips command about double the price that they command inside the United States. So, if a chip costs about $550,000, then they go for about 1 million or more abroad," Groth said.
The theft is the latest in a series of crimes targeting high-value technology shipments in the Bay Area. Last year, police in Fremont and Union City investigated burglaries involving Nvidia cargo valued at more than $7.5 million.
Groth said the scale and complexity of such thefts suggest increasingly sophisticated criminal operations.
"Because the cargoes are getting bigger. The heists are getting more complex and that will point toward a professionalization of the teams that are hijacking these," he said.
An ABC7 viewer also provided video of a separate attempted theft in September. According to police, suspects believed they were targeting trucks carrying expensive Nvidia technology. The trucks instead contained 40,000 pounds of sand.
Groth said the incidents highlight broader concerns about protecting advanced computing technology.
"Security has to get a lot tighter around these because they're a national security asset," he said.
He also raised concerns about where stolen hardware could ultimately end up.
"This is a national security concern as well because we don't know where these chips are going. They could be going to China, they could be anywhere where we have conflict in the world," Groth said.
Authorities have not announced any arrests in the $11.4 million theft, and the investigation remains ongoing.
Experts say the case underscores growing concerns about the security of high-value technology shipments and the potential national security implications when advanced computer hardware enters the black market.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested
articles.title_zh: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested
articles.content_orig:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.
Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse earlier this week of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.
He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
He is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.
Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.
The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, Asunción.
Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.
Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history – a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say Peña is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk Staked His Empire on Texas. Now State Democrats Want to Rein Him In.
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk Staked His Empire on Texas. Now State Democrats Want to Rein Him In.
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk blew $447 million to support Republican candidates in the midterm elections — and almost every single cent of it went to waste .
But if you were about to break out a tiny violin to soundtrack the sorrows of the world’s first — and first former — trillionaire, you should consider acquiring an even tinier one, because those were just the beginning of his losses.
Shares of Musk’s businesses SpaceX and Tesla immediately tanked after Democrats swept the Senate, House, and governorship races — including in Texas, Musk’s base of operations. His automaker fell 3.3 percent, and his rocket-slash-AI company plunged by a full 3.8 , wiping out what Bloomberg reported was over $120 billion.
That did a number on Musk’s personal wealth, which in large part derives from his stakes in those companies. He is now, by the Financial Time’s estimate , some $30 billion poorer.
Despite the excess of egg on his face, Musk still managed to look through his post history on X and start deleting the ones about the election.
Trying to rally his followers, Musk tweeted “Vote red today!” on Tuesday morning. But it was removed after the reality of a blue tsunami came crashing at his doorstep. So was his pinned tweet from last week urging his followers to vote for Republican senators, which according to Forbes was taken down around the time Democratic candidate James Talarico declared victory in the senate race.
To his credit, he did make a few jokes at his own expense.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he tweeted late Tuesday night.
For the most part, though, Musk seems eager to move on. Besides one post in which he claimed “Voter ID failed in California,” he’s gone back to his usual tweets promoting Grok and his various companies almost as if nothing happened. If we spent half a billion dollars trying to get candidates elect who all lost, and were now staring down the barrel of a Democrat-stacked government looking to get revenge on us , we would probably try to sweep everything under the rug, too.
