articles.title_orig: China, EU urged to deepen cooperation amid global transitions
articles.title_zh: China, EU urged to deepen cooperation amid global transitions
articles.content_orig:
China and the European Union should strengthen dialogue, manage their differences and expand cooperation in emerging areas such as artificial intelligence to ensure the stable development of their relationship over the next 50 years, Chinese Ambassador to the EU Cai Run said on Thursday.
Speaking at the 14th China-Europe Forum in Brussels, Cai said the two sides should remain committed to their partnership, resolve economic and trade disputes through consultation, and respect each other's core interests and major concerns.
"We are partners, not rivals, still less adversaries," Cai said. "China is not the source of the economic problems facing the EU, but a partner it can count on in addressing them."
The forum, themed "The Next 50 Years: Navigating Global Transitions in an AI World", was jointly organized by the Chinese Mission to the EU, Brussels-based think tank Friends of Europe and the China Public Diplomacy Association.
Cai said China-EU relations had maintained steady momentum despite challenges. According to Chinese statistics, bilateral trade reached $693.6 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 12.9 percent year-on-year, while two-way investment stock exceeded $290 billion.
He highlighted the progress achieved at the recent second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, where the two sides reached 16 deliverables and understandings covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization reform.
The two sides agreed to hold the third meeting in March next year.
"The agreement on these 16 deliverables and understandings fully demonstrates that both sides have the willingness, capability, and wisdom to resolve issues through dialogue and consultation," Cai said.
Turning to artificial intelligence, Cai said China and the EU possessed distinct strengths and should expand exchanges and cooperation to make AI a new growth area in bilateral relations while jointly advancing global AI governance.
Stefano Grassi, director for external relations at the European Commission's Secretariat-General, highlighted the deep economic ties between China and the EU, noting that China was the EU's third-largest trading partner while the EU is the first export destination for China.
Drawing on his experience during the eurozone debt crisis, Grassi said one of the most important lessons Europe had learned was that correcting economic imbalances required action from both surplus and deficit economies.
He stressed that China and the EU were highly integrated economically, and underscored the importance of jointly addressing economic challenges.
Wu Haitao, vice-president of the China Public Diplomacy Association, also emphasized the importance of dialogue in shaping the next 50 years of China-EU relations.
"Despite our differences, we are all willing to resolve them through dialogue and consultation. This is a very good starting point," Wu said, adding that "differences are inevitable, but how we resolve them matters greatly to both sides".
Against a backdrop of growing geopolitical uncertainty, Wu called on the two sides to play a constructive role in global affairs. "As two major constructive forces in the world, China and the EU should provide stability and certainty to a world marked by turbulence and change," he said.
Cai said China's commitment to high-quality development and high-standard opening-up would create new opportunities for European businesses and other international partners, expressing confidence that joint efforts would help usher in a brighter future for China-EU relations.

Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng held a video call with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Friday, according to information released by the Ministry of Commerce on Saturday.
He, also China's lead representative for China-US economic and trade affairs, held candid, in-depth, and constructive discussions with US officials on major economic and trade issues of mutual concern, focusing on implementing the consensus reached by their heads of state during the meetings in Beijing and Washington, as well as the outcomes of bilateral economic and trade consultations.
During the talks, the Chinese side expressed serious concerns over recent US economic and trade restrictions targeting China.
Both sides agreed to continue making effective use of the bilateral economic and trade consultation mechanism under the strategic guidance of their heads of state, deepen cooperation, and properly manage differences.
They also agreed to promote sustained, stable, and positive development of bilateral economic and trade relations, contributing to a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity.

articles.title_orig: Russian forces launch missile attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv, mayor says
articles.title_zh: Russian forces launch missile attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv, mayor says
articles.content_orig:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Missile explosions struck Kyiv and left at least five people injured early on Saturday as Ukraine prepared for new talks next week with Russia and the United States.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, following the most recent round in Geneva in February.
Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.
The Russian missiles that hit the Ukrainian capital overnight damaged homes and commercial properties, closed traffic on a Kyiv bridge over the Dnipro River and triggered new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.
“As a result of the enemy’s night attack, energy facilities in the Kyiv and ... Zhytomyr regions were damaged,” Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. “The situation with the capital’s energy supply is extremely difficult, affecting the city’s heating and water supply systems.”
Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
Dozens of people remain missing after 55 were killed — two of the bodies were recovered early Saturday — in the attack on the former school turned aid distribution center.
The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq, S&P 500 and AI Stocks Rebound After Brutal Week
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq, S&P 500 and AI Stocks Rebound After Brutal Week
articles.content_orig:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre BaquÃ©, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title_orig: New Zealanders head to polls on final day of voting
articles.title_zh: New Zealanders head to polls on final day of voting
articles.content_orig:
Polls have opened on the final day of voting in New Zealand against a backdrop of concerns over the rising cost of living and the broader state of the economy.
Polling stations opened at 9am on Saturday (20:00 GMT Friday) and close at 7pm (06:00 GMT Saturday).
Voting already began on October 26. More than 1.6 million voters, out of nearly 3.8 million in total, had cast their ballots by the end of Thursday, according to the country’s Electoral Commission.
The country has strict laws banning any talk of politics on election day.
The 19-hour election day blackout, which ends when polling places close on Saturday evening, bars everyone, including political parties, news outlets and social media users, from commenting on likely election outcomes, campaign issues and anything else that might encourage or discourage people from voting in a particular way.
Billboards and advertising must be removed. Bumper stickers, T-shirts and even social media profile pictures are also covered by the law.
Breaches of the law can incur a fine of up to 20,000 New Zealand dollars ($11,000).
Opinion polls ahead of the tightly contested election suggest the governing centre-right National Party and the opposition centre-left Labour Party neck and neck, with neither on course to win enough seats to govern alone.
New Zealand’s Electoral Commission aims to release preliminary results from 95 percent of polling stations by the end of election night on Saturday. A final result, which will reflect ballots cast by New Zealanders abroad, is expected by November 27.
Most parties are campaigning on the economy, but their suggested solutions differ widely.
The National Party is pledging to return the budget to surplus through fiscal discipline while expanding the national pension scheme.
The Labour Party is focusing on the cost of living, promising cheaper healthcare and transport.
Recent polls show no clear winner. A handful of seats either way could decide who governs.
New Zealand holds a general election every three years under a mixed-member proportional system.
Voters do not elect a leader of the country but instead select a local electorate candidate and a political party.
Electorate winners earn a seat in the typically 120-seat parliament, as do the highest-ranked members of the party based on their national party vote.

The dedicated Action button will allegedly start disappearing from new iPhones in the second half of 2027. Its functions will move to the Camera Control, with a single press opening the Camera app and a long press triggering the shortcut assigned to the Action button. The tipster specifically stresses that it's the Action button going away, not the camera key.

We've previously heard that next year's Pro models could feature a more substantial redesign, with quad-curved screens being tested in prototypes . Whether the rumored button change is part of that redesign remains to be seen.

articles.title_orig: US urges China to honour Busan trade deal commitments
articles.title_zh: US urges China to honour Busan trade deal commitments
articles.content_orig:
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to urge Beijing to immediately implement commitments under the Busan trade agreement.
“Secretary Bessent emphasised the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments made in Busan and raised concerns about recent Chinese actions. He underscored that continued progress depends on concrete results and that the United States will closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement,” the US Department of the Treasury said in a statement announcing the discussions on Friday.
The announcement refers to a trade deal negotiated between Washington and Beijing in which US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to ease tariffs and lift restrictions on tech to de-escalate tensions amid tit-for-tat tariffs imposed first by Washington and then by Beijing.
On Thursday, China said it was open to buying more US farm goods if the world’s two largest economies agreed to implement the reciprocal tariff cut.
“China has consistently been open to expanding purchases of agricultural products from the US, but only on the condition that the two sides implement their agreed ’30 billion for 30 billion’ reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement,” Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson Huang Ling said in a statement.
The move follows a September meeting between Trump and Xi, when the White House proposed $60bn in cuts, including $17bn worth of US farm goods.
In May, the White House said Beijing agreed to buy $17bn of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year’s target adjusted on a prorated basis. Those purchases were in addition to a commitment made last October to buy US soya beans.
“Secretary Bessent reiterated the Trump Administration’s commitment to pursuing trade and economic policies that benefit American workers, farmers, and businesses and strengthen U.S. economic and national security,” the Treasury added.

articles.title_orig: A Retiree Who Bought 1,000 Oracle Shares at $39 Just Watched Microsoft Walk Away
articles.title_zh: A Retiree Who Bought 1,000 Oracle Shares at $39 Just Watched Microsoft Walk Away
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Microsoft is winding down an AI computing rental deal with Oracle. The stock hit a one-year low of $109.21, then closed up 0.8% at $116.10.
A retiree's 1,000 shares, bought for $39,090 in 2016, are worth $116,100, down from $328,330 at the September 2025 peak.
Selling 300 shares would cut Oracle from 12.7% to 8.9% of the portfolio for about $3,465 in federal tax.
Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)
Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) shareholders got one more piece of bad news on Friday. Bloomberg reported that Microsoft is winding down a deal to rent artificial intelligence computing capacity from Oracle, after declining to renew the contract. Oracle stock fell as low as $109.21, down 5.2% from Thursday's close and its lowest price in more than a year. Then buyers stepped in, and the stock finished the day up 0.8% at $116.10.
That bounce does little for anyone who has owned Oracle for a while. The stock closed at $328.33 on Sept. 10, 2025. At Friday's close it was 64.6% below that peak, 40.7% lower for the year and 11.2% lower for the week alone.
Take a 66-year-old retiree who bought 1,000 shares on Nov. 7, 2016, at $39.09 a share, a $39,090 investment. Those shares were worth $328,330 at the peak. On Friday they were worth $116,100. They also collect $2,700 a month from Social Security and hold another $800,000 in retirement savings, so Oracle is now 12.7% of a $916,100 portfolio. The question in front of them is whether this week's news is a reason to sell.
The deal dates to 2023. Oracle agreed to provide Microsoft with server capacity to power a new AI-assisted version of the Bing search engine. According to Bloomberg, Microsoft has been switching that rented capacity off in recent months because the older-generation chips inside Oracle's hardware no longer fit its needs. The full size of the deal was never disclosed.
If you've saved over $1,000,000, this guide is for you. The last thing you want in retirement is to run out of money, you want your money to generate lasting income while you enjoy your life.
Now you can learn the strategies wealthy retirees use to fund their retirement with The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income from Fisher Investments. Download the guide today! (sponsor)
Oracle did not deny the report. A company spokesperson said demand for its AI cloud infrastructure "remains strong," including for earlier-generation chips, and Oracle said in September that it was renewing contracts for four-year-old chips at a 20% premium to the original price.
The report landed in a week that had already been rough for Oracle shareholders:
Monday, Nov. 2: the stock fell 8.8% after Oracle announced plans to raise $20 billion, half through new stock and half through bonds.
Thursday, Nov. 5: it fell another 6.9% as artificial intelligence stocks sold off across the market.
Friday, Nov. 6: it fell as much as 5.2% on the Microsoft report, then recovered to close up 0.8%.
Measured from the purchase, the investment still looks good. The 1,000 shares cost $39,090 and are worth $116,100, a gain of $77,010, or 197%. Oracle has also paid $12.85 a share in dividends since that purchase, or $12,850 on 1,000 shares. Today it pays 50 cents a share each quarter, $2,000 a year on this position, a yield of 1.72% at Friday's price.
Measured from the peak, the same shares have given back $212,230. That is the number that keeps most long-term holders up at night, and it is the wrong one to anchor on. The $328,330 was never cash. The decision in front of this retiree is about the $116,100 that exists today.
Oracle's business is still growing quickly. In its most recent quarter, revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion and cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% to $7.4 billion. Its backlog of signed contracts reached $664 billion.
The stock is also far cheaper than it was. At $116.10, Oracle trades at about 18 times its earnings over the past year and about 15 times what analysts expect it to earn next year. Of the 43 analysts tracked, 35 rate it a buy or strong buy, and their average price target is $235.46, about double Friday's close.
Warren Buffett's oldest rule applies here. He has quoted his teacher Benjamin Graham for decades: "Price is what you pay; value is what you get." A stock that has fallen 65% can be a better value than it was at the top, if the business behind it is still sound.
The worries are about how Oracle is paying for its growth. The company spent $55.7 billion on equipment and data centers in its 2026 fiscal year, its total debt has reached $167 billion, and analysts expect it to burn more cash than it brings in through its 2028 fiscal year. The $20 billion raise this week added more stock and more debt on top of that.
The backlog is also concentrated. According to S&P, a single AI customer accounts for about half of the $664 billion. Microsoft's decision is small next to that, but it shows that customers can and do walk away from AI computing deals that no longer fit.
For a retiree, one stock at 12.7% of everything they own is a large bet. A further 50% drop would cost about $58,000, which is almost two years of the $32,400 Social Security pays them.
Selling part of the position is a reasonable option for this retiree. If they sell 300 of the 1,000 shares at Friday's price:
Taxable gain: $23,103, since each share cost $39.09
Federal tax at the 15% long-term rate: about $3,465
What remains: 700 shares worth $81,270, or 8.9% of the portfolio, still paying $1,400 a year in dividends
If the shares sit in a traditional IRA instead of a taxable account, there is no tax on the sale itself, and the trim costs nothing today.
That keeps most of the upside if the analysts are right and cuts the damage if this week turns out to be the start of something worse. It also turns a portion of a paper gain into cash, which is the gain that actually pays bills.
Microsoft walking away from an Oracle AI deal is a real headline, and the stock's quick recovery on Friday shows the market did not treat it as a disaster. For a 66-year-old who turned $39,090 into $116,100 over 10 years and collected $12,850 in dividends along the way, the bigger question is how much of their retirement should ride on one company. Selling 300 shares would cut Oracle to 8.9% of the portfolio for about $3,465 in tax, and the remaining 700 shares would keep paying $1,400 a year.

articles.title_orig: US Treasury sanctions Canadian money services firms over Iran-related transactions
articles.title_zh: US Treasury sanctions Canadian money services firms over Iran-related transactions
articles.content_orig:
The United States government has announced sanctions against several Canadian currency-exchange businesses accused of helping the Iranian regime and, in several cases, also helping the alleged head of a drug trafficking ring.
The U.S. Department of the Treasury on Friday said eight Canadian businesses had helped Iranian entities get around financial sanctions. It said some also helped launder proceeds of crime by changing Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets, like crypto.
"Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies," Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wrote in a statement.
Toronto businessman accused in U.S. of helping Iran's regime was also investigated in Canada
The sanctions effectively cut the Canadian firms off from the U.S. dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets ​the firms might have south of the border and banning any ​transactions with American people or entities.
In its statement, the treasury said the crackdown is part of a wider effort to "sever the economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime" and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which is listed as a terrorist organization in Canada .
The Treasury identified the sanctioned businesses in Ontario and British Columbia as the following:
The statement said the companies gave the Iranian regime "financial lifelines" by providing their services. In several cases, officials said the businesses have changed their names and addresses to avoid detection.
In August, the Trump administration expanded secondary sanctions its government can impose on ‌entities and countries maintaining business connections with Iran, raising the economic pressure on Tehran as the war neared its six-month mark.
"​Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran ⁠stands alone," Bessent said at the time.
Trump administration expands U.S. sanctions on Iran targeting countries with business ties to Tehran
In addition, the statement said three of those businesses helped Ryan Wedding — the Olympian-turned-alleged-drug-kingpin — hide money by laundering bulk cash into digital assets. Ultimately, the treasury said companies sent millions of dollars worth of digital funds abroad before Wedding was arrested in January .
CBC News has contacted Wedding's lawyer for comment.

Her work over the past decade has taken her across North America, from the Canadian Rockies to Washington, D.C. articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV, who had cancer surgery just weeks ago, begins grueling South American tour
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV, who had cancer surgery just weeks ago, begins grueling South American tour
articles.content_orig:
ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT — Three countries in 12 days, a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses on a trip covering around 19,000 miles. Less than a month after Pope Leo XIV underwent cancer surgery , he set off on what the Vatican called a “homecoming” tour of South America.
The 71-year-old’s long trip across the strongly Catholic region will take him to Uruguay and Argentina, as well as to Peru, where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.
Leo considers the tour, one of the most grueling undertaken by a Catholic leader in decades, a “homecoming to places where he spent a long time and to which he feels closely connected,” Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni told journalists at a briefing Tuesday.
The Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday that he was ⁠hoping to “strengthen the faith, renew hope” and “rekindle the fire of charity.”
Leo will hold several meetings with survivors of sexual abuse by ​Catholic clergy during the trip, the Vatican has said, without yet providing further details.
Bruni said the pope would also address a range of issues facing the continent, including environmental destruction, ⁠arms trafficking and regional political instability, bringing “a message of communion and unity.”
Leo departed from Rome’s Fiumicino Airport early ​Friday, and arrived in Uruguay on Friday afternoon for the country’s first papal visit since 1988.
After takeoff, Leo told journalists aboard the plane that he had no doubt he would embark on the trip.
“I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place. I confess that from the first day I had no doubt,” he said. “I was convinced that this trip had to go forward and very happy to say, praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistants, I am here today, I think, in fairly good shape.”
Asked if he had any advice for other people facing cancer, Leo replied, “Not to be afraid, early detection is obviously the best way to go, regular check ups and take care of yourself.”
Leo also noted that “trust in God, good doctors, good surgeons, and, overall, a healthy lifestyle” had contributed to his quick recovery.
Leo, who is the first pope to vote in a U.S. election, was also asked about the importance of voting.
“I am proud to be an American and to exercise my right,” he said.
Considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people go to Mass regularly, Uruguay was the first in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use and the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion.
In October 2025, the country of just 3.5 million people became the first in the region to approve legislation for assisted dying despite strong opposition from the Catholic Church.
After Uruguay, Leo’s tour will take him to Argentina for three days, where he is expected to meet with right-wing President Javier Milei , a close ally of President Donald Trump .
It will be the first papal visit to Argentina since Pope John Paul II traveled to the country in 1987.
Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was born in Argentina, the first pontiff from the region, but he declined numerous invitations to return to his homeland.
The biggest crowds of the trip are likely next week during his six-day visit to Peru, where Leo is widely celebrated as a beloved national figure. He will stop off in the capital, Lima, before visiting his former diocese of Chiclayo, where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until taking up a Vatican post in 2023.
Leo, who was treated last month for lung ‌adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, will also make several high-altitude visits in the Peruvian Andes.
Doctors have ⁠said that the disease was localized and that he would not require any further treatments; Bruni said Leo had recovered enough that no additional medical measures ⁠would be necessary during his trip.
Speaking at the same briefing Tuesday, Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief, said Leo was grateful for the concern about his health and the demands the journey might make on him.
But, she said, he was “so excited” to make the trip.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_zh: Russian ballistic missiles slam Kyiv after Zelensky warns of mass attack
articles.content_orig:
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Several waves of Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv overnight on Nov. 6-7, just hours after President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia was preparing another large-scale infrastructure attack.
At least two people in the city of Kyiv have been wounded, along with a third victim in the surrounding region, according to authorities.
As Ukraine's Air Force warned that ballistic missiles were bound for the capital, a series of explosions rocked the city, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
The first barrage of missiles attacked Kyiv in quick succession, with the Air Force reporting that at least six missiles were launched at the city in the span of a few minutes shortly before 11 p.m. local time on Nov. 6.
Residents received an all-clear signal about 30 minutes later. But the respite was brief, with another aerial alert coming shortly before midnight. A fresh missile wave targeted the city shortly after 1 a.m., with Kyiv Independent journalists reporting another round of at least six loud blasts.
At least two people have been injured, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration. The victims are receiving medical treatment.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported explosions in the suburbs and warned that Russia was attacking infrastructure facilities with ballistic missiles.
Later, the mayor reported damage to a five-story residential building in the city's Solomianskyi district and shattered windows at another five-story building at an unspecified location. Emergency services have been dispatched to both scenes, he said.
A fire also broke out at a non-residential building in the Solomianskyi district, the Kyiv City Military Administration said . A kindergarten in the same district was also damaged by the attack.
Explosions again rocked the city at 3:04 a.m. local time, a Kyiv Independent journalist on the ground reported.
The wave of explosions continued with ballistic missiles targeting the city at 3:30 a.m. local time, a reporter said.
The full extent of the consequences is not yet clear. Attacks remain ongoing at the time of publication.
Outside of the city, Kyiv Oblast Governor Tymur Tkachenko reported that a Russian jet-powered drone attack in the Brovary district caused a fire in a home, injuring one victim. The man was extracted from the rubble of the damaged building and has been hospitalized due to burns and multiple shrapnel wounds.
Earlier in the evening, Zelensky told Ukrainians that intelligence reports point to another massive Russian strike on infrastructure. The attack will likely target bridges, energy facilities, and civilian infrastructure, he warned.
Kyiv, a city the size of Berlin with a population of 3 million, has come under relentless assault in recent weeks as Russia begins its annual campaign against Ukraine's power grid. The city endured the largest strike on energy this year on Nov. 3, leading to widespread blackouts and water supply cutoffs.
As residents suffer, city officials and the central government have traded blame for the worsening state of Kyiv's energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
Ukraine struck various sites in the Russian regions of Oryol, Saratov, and Rostov, hitting an oil refinery among several targets overnight on Nov. 7, monitoring channels reported.
At least three people have been injured in the city and the surrounding region. Damage has been reported at homes, apartment buildings, and a kindergarten.

articles.title_orig: Investors try to regain their footing after tech stocks tank
articles.title_zh: Investors try to regain their footing after tech stocks tank
articles.content_orig:
Tech stocks in the U.S. steadied Friday after suffering one of their worst routs in years, as investors weighed the prospect of an AI investment slowdown resulting from Democratic midterm victories against the sector’s long-term growth potential.
The tech-focused Nasdaq 100 closed up 1.1% after plunging 6.3% on Thursday, its worst single-day performance since the Covid-19 pandemic.
The broader S&P 500 finished 0.3% higher, after tanking 4.4% Thursday, a drop that wiped out $2.8 trillion worth of wealth on paper.
A strong October jobs report Friday morning increased the odds that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its next policy meeting in December. The prospect of higher borrowing costs helped to push stocks down from their highs earlier in the day.
Investors continue to digest the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which a crop of Democratic candidates were elected to office who had pledged to rein in AI and data centers . They include Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa of Texas, a state that is among the largest data center markets in the country.
The AI boom is responsible for an ever-increasing share of U.S. stock market gains and economic growth, so any threat to the narrative of demand-fueled growth can rattle investors.
“Markets are being punished according to their dependence on the U.S. AI infrastructure cycle,” Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Singapore-based SAXO Markets, told NBC News.
The incoming Democratic-controlled Congress could also tighten scrutiny of the AI industry, including its infrastructure projects, which could cause delays and additional costs.
This would add to existing worries investors already have about the long-term profitability of these investments.
Some analysts viewed Thursday’s dramatic sell-off as overblown —  merely a sign of some froth coming off an overstretched market —  rather than the end of the line for the AI investment boom.
Recent declines are “just speed bumps,” said economist and investor Ed Yardeni.
Rather than spelling doom for the sector, Yardeni said losses like this week’s could ultimately help keep the AI bubble from overheating.
Until it becomes clearer how much data center construction is truly threatened by newly elected lawmakers, volatility is likely to continue.
“This is a stock market that is trying to figure out the right valuations for the AI trade, which is grappling with a swift sentiment shift after the midterm elections,” said Alex Guiliano, chief investment officer at New Jersey-based Resonate Wealth Partners.
Friday kicked off with steep losses in Asia. Japan’s Nikkei suffered its worst week since 2020, falling as much as 6% and more than 20% since its most recent high, putting it in bear-market territory. South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled more than 8%, triggering a temporary market-wide trading halt. There, AI data center memory suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix plunged more than 10% in the early hours, before recovering some of their losses.
In Taiwan, home to some of the most critical AI companies, including chip supplier TSMC, the benchmark TAIEX index dropped 9%.
The companies in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan are linked to the global AI spending cycle and “hence I am not surprised to see the magnitude of correction today following the sharp correction in the U.S.,” Tai Hui, J.P. Morgan’s APAC chief market strategist, told NBC News in emailed comments.
The months leading up to the American elections had already been a rollercoaster for Asian investors, who saw their fortunes soar in June during the AI stock boom, but have been suffering from a brutal recent sell-off.
A sense that valuations of key AI companies were inflated was troublesome enough for markets in Asia, but the Democratic sweep has introduced another layer of uncertainty.
Markets had largely expected losses for Trump’s Republicans, but not on this scale.
“This matters enormously for Asia because much of the hardware supporting America’s AI ambitions is manufactured here,” Chanana, from SAXO Markets, said.
In China, both the tech-focused Star 50 and the AI Index slumped as much as 5% before recouping some losses.
“There is a legitimate argument that parts of China’s AI equity bubble have already burst,” Chanana said.
But she added that unlike the U.S., where much of the investment is commercially driven, “China treats AI and semiconductor self-sufficiency as strategic national priorities.”
“This means investment can continue for reasons beyond immediate profitability, including technological independence, industrial competitiveness and national security.”
That is not the case in South Korea, whose market darlings, memory makers SK Hynix and Samsung, are an integral part of the commercial AI buildout. That makes the country particularly sensitive to any U.S. slowdowns.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index more than doubled in market value in June, but by Friday had shed most of the gains made this year. Like South Korea, there is acute exposure for Taiwan — key for advanced chip manufacturing and TSMC’s headquarters.
Nevertheless, most of the Asian indexes are still higher than they were a year ago: South Korea’s Kospi is up 25%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 is up 13%, and TSEC Taiwan Technology is also up by 47%.
“For semiconductor and memory makers in Asia Pacific, as long as global demand for computing power continues to grow, demand for the underlying hardware should remain healthy over the medium term,” J.P. Morgan’s Hui said.
“There may be constraints on where the ‘gold’ can be mined, but as long as demand for the gold remains, the picks and shovels will still be needed elsewhere,” he added.
Mithil Aggarwal is a Hong Kong-based reporter/producer for NBC News.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
articles.title_zh: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
articles.content_orig:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre BaquÃ©, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title_orig: AI data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
articles.title_zh: AI data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
articles.content_orig:
The artificial intelligence data center boom hit a roadblock on election night , further complicating the tech industry's historic expansion plans.
There were 41 local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, according to Ballotpedia .
Voters sided against data centers in each measure except one in Harwood, North Dakota, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. The lone exception was Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected an added review of industrial projects, including data centers.
Ohio alone accounted for more than half of the measures, with 21 on the ballot. The issue also played out at the top of the ticket, where Democrat Sherrod Brown ousted Republican Sen. Jon Husted after casting the incumbent as "the face of data centers."
The Buckeye State, which was named America's Top State for Business in 2026 by CNBC, has become a key battleground for the issue.
OpenAI announced in August that it secured 8 gigawatts of computing capacity at the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio, the largest planned AI data center campus in the world. The first phase of construction is slated to begin this year, and capacity is expected to come online in phases starting in 2028, according to the project's website .
SoftBank and SB Energy are developing the Ohio data center campus in partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy. SoftBank is a major investor in OpenAI, and the two companies announced plans to invest $1 billion in SB Energy earlier this year.
Nvidia is backstopping the project, which could cost more than $500 billion in total.
Those plans could now run into resistance from the governor's mansion. Ohio's top office flipped blue on Tuesday, as Democrat Amy Acton, a physician, defeated Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy. Acton supports a "conditional moratorium" on data centers to ensure they cover 100% of utility costs and "exclusively build with union labor."
Heading into the election, the AI trade was already faltering on Wall Street, with chipmakers, neoclouds and other data center-related companies selling off in October on concerns about rising interest rates and overspending. The hyperscalers — Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft and Meta — are each spending hundreds of billions of dollars a year on AI infrastructure to meet what they say is insatiable demand. All of those companies except Microsoft have turned cash flow negative in the process.
Getting data center projects off the ground may have just gotten a lot harder.
Communities in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, New Jersey, Nevada and Wisconsin also went to the polls to weigh in on the issue, according to Ballotpedia, and data centers were a key motivating factor for voters in matters up and down the ballot.
In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, with Democrats ranking the issue higher than Republicans.
Democrats who campaigned on pausing or regulating new projects won key races in Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia and Texas, which is on track to become the world's largest data center market by 2030.
In one of the most significant results of the night for Democrats, Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott after blaming the Republican incumbent for the rapid buildout of data centers across Texas, saying he put the tech industry's interests ahead of local communities.
The losses came despite record spending from Silicon Valley to shape the 2026 midterms, with the GOP boasting a commanding advantage among the election's biggest donors. According to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records, 14 of the 20 largest donor groups backed Republicans almost exclusively. Crypto, AI and online gambling interests poured in more than $377 million.
Elon Musk , the cycle’s largest individual donor, spent at least $474 million, nearly half of it in Texas, and lost both of the state’s marquee races. It was a warning sign for the wave of tech companies and founders who left California for Texas in search of a friendlier business climate.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote in a post on X.
Within hours of the polls closing, Democrats were already calling for AI executives to testify under oath.
Among the first to seize on the results was Rep. Greg Casar, the Texas Democrat who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus.
"The House Democratic majority must make it a top priority to protect Americans' jobs, freedom, and lives from AI billionaires," Casar said in a statement after Democrats were projected to win the House. "AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath."
Casar also accused Republicans of being "bought and paid for by AI billionaires," arguing that voters had rejected that influence and warning Democrats to "hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks."
He said the data center fight is only the beginning.
"The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election," he said. "And in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics."
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the presumptive next chair of the House Oversight Committee, summed it up in two words: "Lawyer up."
— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: The Taipei Mayor Election Is Not About China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The Taipei Mayor Election Is Not About China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
In October, well-known Taiwanese television host Kevin Tsai, popular on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, was spotted by the media attending a campaign event for Puma Shen, a legislator running for mayor of Taipei. Given Tsai’s popularity in China, his appearance quickly sparked criticism. The incumbent Taipei mayor, Chiang Wan-an, helped defuse the controversy by inviting Tsai to the opening of his own campaign headquarters. Three weeks after attending Shen’s campaign event, Tsai publicly stated that he had never supported Taiwanese independence and that his work required him to interact with people holding a range of political views. The following day, he attended Chiang’s campaign event.
If attending a rally is tantamount to declaring one’s support for Taiwan’s future, imagine what will be made of the November 28 vote.
Shen, the candidate of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), has spent years studying Chinese influence operations and promoting civilian preparedness in Taiwan. Chinese authorities have opened an investigation into him on allegations of secession. Chiang, the Kuomintang (KMT) incumbent, has maintained an open channel of communication between officials in Taipei and Shanghai. Beijing and Washington may be tempted to interpret a Shen victory as a vote for independence or a Chiang victory as a turn toward China. Either interpretation, however, would link a municipal election to an issue that Taipei’s voters have not been asked to vote on.
Consider an exchange during the October 31 debate between Shen and Chiang. Chiang challenged Shen to explain why two redevelopment projects, one in Datong and the other in Neihu, had stalled. Chiang attributed the delays to restrictions on building heights near Taipei’s Songshan Airport. Shen fired back with a question of his own: If city officials knew about these restrictions, why hadn’t they explained them to residents from the outset? Chiang used the exchange to question his challenger’s command of city affairs. Shen, in turn, used it to ask what good that expertise did residents if they learned about an obstacle too late to do anything about it.
The most important takeaway from their heated exchanges, however, is not what the candidates said, but what they left unsaid. China, the elephant in the room when it comes to cross-strait relations, was not raised even once as a key issue during the two-hour debate.
That encapsulates the kind of local issues Taipei voters will actually base their decision on. Some might vote for Chiang, crediting him with moving other difficult projects forward, including one at Nanjichang Night Market. Others might favor Shen’s proposal to screen older buildings for earthquake risks and to help residents arrange repairs. Two homeowners could vote for different candidates – while holding precisely the same views about China. The election night count offers no way to tell.
Taipei’s recent electoral history illustrates the limits of interpreting local elections through the lens of national politics – and vice versa. In 2022, the city elected Chiang as mayor. Just over a year later, in the presidential election, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te carried Taipei, edging out the KMT’s Hou Yu-ih by just 641 votes. Chiang’s mayoral victory would therefore have been a poor guide to the city’s presidential preferences. There is even less reason to interpret a vote in the capital as evidence of a broader change of heart across Taiwan for or against a political party – or that party’s approach to China.
True, the result will shape national politics. Winning Taipei would give Shen a larger audience for his work on civilian defense. A second term would give Chiang greater standing within the KMT to make the case for engagement with Shanghai, and possibly Beijing. Plus, the Taipei mayorship has in the past served as a launching pad for presidential ambitions. Winning office gives a politician the chance to advance causes that may have had little to do with why voters chose him.
The election’s outcome could certainly also influence cross-strait relations. During Chiang’s tenure, the Taipei–Shanghai Twin-City Forum has kept officials from the two cities in contact. A Chiang victory would give him another term to pursue those exchanges. A Shen victory would test the conditions under which they can continue. Although Shen has criticized the forum’s value, he has said he would attend if it offered practical benefits and came without political preconditions. On October 14, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office dismissed his offer, citing his alleged support for independence.
Suppose Shen wins, repeats his offer, and finds Shanghai unwilling to meet with him. Concluding that Taipei voters chose to sever contact would erase Beijing’s role in the decision. The reverse inference – that vote for Chiang implies approval of his engagement with Chinese officials – would be equally questionable. A Taipei resident might value Chiang’s ability to keep municipal officials talking while still opposing closer political ties. Wanting the conversation with Shanghai to continue is entirely compatible with wanting Beijing to have less say in Taiwan’s affairs.
Local governance is undoubtedly important for the stability of the Taiwan Strait. Taipei’s city government, for example, helps residents prepare for an air raid, down to practicing how to reach shelter when the sirens sound. How well the city carries out that work matters regardless of which party holds power. Still, it’s not going to be an issue that is top of mind when Taipei residents fill out their ballots.
On November 28, Taipei’s voters will choose who takes responsibility for the safety of their homes, the city’s readiness for an emergency, and its dealings with Shanghai. Beijing and Washington have good reason to pay close attention to what the next mayor does with that authority. But anyone claiming a mandate for independence or unification is looking for evidence the mayoral count cannot provide.

Ping Ping, a male, and Fu Shuang, a female, arrived in September from China under a 10-year loan agreement, bringing the cuddly black-and-white bears back to the zoo after a two-year absence.
After spending the past weeks getting acclimated to their habitat, the six-year-old pandas greeted visitors in the newly renovated Arthur M. Blank Panda Grove.

articles.title_orig: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
articles.title_zh: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
articles.content_orig:
European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.
Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.
The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.
Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.
The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) said on Friday it had begun conducting investigative measures at Spain's rail authorities "after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line".
The EPPO highlighted high public interest in the case, but said no further details would be made public.
As part of the process, a Spanish judge assigned to the case has to ensure the investigation complies with legal safeguards, including authorising any measures that might involve house searches or phone-tapping.
The Urda disaster has damaged the Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez ahead of a 29 November general election and the party is trailing the conservative People's Party (PP) in most opinion polls.
Close Sánchez ally Óscar Puente resigned this week as transport minister, after seeing two deadly accidents on his watch this year.
The PP and far-right Vox say Puente's resignation is not enough and they have demanded that Sánchez resign too.
Many people in Spain have now become wary of taking the train, with reports of widespread cancellations and empty station platforms.
A funeral for the 69 victims at Urda will take place on Tuesday at Toledo cathedral, in the same province that the disaster happened.
Puente's successor, Carlos Cuerpo, has vowed to take all necessary measures to "restore the confidence of Spaniards in our high-speed rail".
Cuerpo met survivors of January's Adamuz disaster on Friday and they handed him a list of 11 demands for improving safety on Spain's railways.

articles.title_orig: US and Iran Edge Closer to Deal With Nuclear Issue Back in Play
articles.title_zh: US and Iran Edge Closer to Deal With Nuclear Issue Back in Play
articles.content_orig:
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that aid provided by the U.S. has been used by Israel "both to defend itself and to confront enemies who threaten America and the West."
"U.S. military aid to Israel has always been a cross-the-aisle agreement," the office wrote on X after President Donald Trump announced earlier this week that $4 billion in aid would be "cut off at the end of the year."
"Today, Israel has a strong and stable economy. The move by PM Netanyahu and President Trump from aid to partnership shows the strength and sophistication of our relationship, and its ability to adapt and stand strong over time," Netanyahu's office added.
Trump said on Election Day, "Israel's our number one," and, "We give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it."
President Donald Trump said Friday that "Israel and, in fact, the entire Middle East, WOULD NOT EXIST TODAY if I did not stop Iran from having a Nuclear Weapon.
"Nobody wants to say that, but everybody knows it’s true!" the president added in a post on Truth Social.
Trump made the remark after announcing earlier this week that $4 billion in U.S. aid to Israel would be "cut off" by the end of the year.
An Iranian military official vowed Friday that any country helping the U.S. in a potential new attack on Iran would become a legitimate target, a report said.
Brig. Gen. Ali Balali, who is a senior advisor to the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force, also said Friday that Iran's missiles have enough range to strike U.S. and Israeli targets, according to Iran's Tasnim News Agency.
The remarks come after reports emerged last week that movements were being made in the Middle East to give President Donald Trump options if he decided to pursue further military action against Iran following Tuesday's midterm elections.
Russia played a larger role in the Iran war than previously disclosed, with internal defense industry documents revealing how Moscow built up the country's arsenal ahead of its conflict with the U.S.
A Russian contract is tied to 90 launchers for precision-guided missiles with the destination as Tehran, according to documents obtained and published by Ukrainian defense intelligence research group Dallas Analytics offering new details on the extent of Moscow's military support for Iran before war erupted.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly downplayed Russia's role in the conflict — as recently as last month, saying that he did not believe they are helping Iran "at all."
Russian production records show components were allocated for 90 APU-L twin-rail launchers under a contract identified as "K-10," with shipments within the Russian production chain scheduled from late 2024 through December 2025.
Other internal Russian documents obtained by Dallas Analytics explicitly identify "K-10" as Iran. An October 2022 supply request for equipment for a Yak-130 aircraft lists the consignee as "'K10' Iran" and was countersigned by the acting head of the Russian Defense Ministry's 704th Military Representation.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said Friday that eight ships have been attacked so far this week in the Strait of Hormuz.
Since July 6, a total of 63 of 88 projectile strikes happened along a southern route near the coastline of Oman, according to the UKMTO.
There were also three ships attacked this week in the Arabian Gulf, it added.
"Of the 11 incidents, 3 continued their voyage, 5 required assistance and 3 Vessels sunk," the UKMTO said in a weekly overview, noting that the risk for ships traveling through the Strait of Hormuz remains "severe."
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., accused Pete Hegseth of "wasting taxpayer dollars" after the secretary of war posted a video to social media Thursday defending the Iran war and calling on Congress to approve a $350 billion budget request.
"Pete Hegseth, cabinet secretaries shouldn't be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos. Kristi Noem learned that the hard way," Tillis said in a post on X Friday.
"This is about you: the incompetence you’ve displayed, the bad advice you’ve given to the president, and your shameful and embarrassing episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters," he added.
Tillis previously has called on President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth.
Ali Akbar Velayati, an advisor to Iran's supreme leader on international affairs, said Friday that, "Any energy or transit corridor that tries to bypass us will either become too expensive or unstable."
"Now that everyone is talking about the new order of West Asia, it should be noted that: Iran is a bridge between [the] Persian Gulf, Central Asia, Caucasus, and the Sea of Oman," he added on X.
"The domino effect of crises from Gaza to the Red Sea, and from Lebanon to Iraq, has shown that regional security is indivisible," Velayati said. "Either collective security is achieved, or everyone experiences collective insecurity."
“The tsunami of geopolitical changes in West Asia has engulfed the elections in Israel and the United States. The result: ‘Iran is now one of the principal architects of the regional order — a reality that can neither be eliminated nor replaced’,” Velayati also was quoted as saying Friday by Iran's Tasnim News Agency.
Vice President JD Vance privately accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of being "wrong on everything" about the Iran war, according to reports, as disagreements over the conflict expose tensions within the Trump administration and raise questions about Vance's potential 2028 presidential ambitions.
The clash, reported by Axios Nov. 4., comes after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections and Vance publicly blamed the war for the party's defeat while urging President Donald Trump to pursue a negotiated settlement rather than renewed military strikes.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote later on Wednesday on X.
"Low-level hostility between Vance and Netanyahu is beneficial for Vance," Natan Sachs, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, told Fox News Digital.
"It allows him to give some distance from the Trump administration, which has just taken a huge electoral beating, but also to position himself ... in a very different position than President Trump himself without attacking Trump."
Qatar said Friday that President Donald Trump called its leader Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani to discuss "the ongoing diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions in the region."
The state-run Qatar News Agency said Al-Thani and Trump "discussed the latest international efforts, notably the initiatives led by the State of Qatar, to bridge the gaps between the concerned parties and support the negotiation process, to pave the road for reaching a comprehensive agreement that resolves the crisis and ensures security and stability in the region."
The call comes as Qatar is acting as a mediator in talks between the U.S. and Iran that are aimed at ending the war.
Qatar said Al-Thani also "emphasized the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes; preventing further escalation in the region; and safeguarding freedom of maritime navigation and the security of energy supplies."
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said Friday that a tanker ship traveling through the Strait of Hormuz reported an explosion.
The incident happened Thursday about 16 nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman, the agency said.
"The Master of a Tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz outbound, has reported an explosion at the waterline, port side," the UKTMO said. "The crew are safe and are accounted for. The tanker is still under its own power and is continuing on its voyage."

articles.title_orig: Where China Sees the Danger in a Wounded Trump
articles.title_zh: Where China Sees the Danger in a Wounded Trump
articles.content_orig:
China won’t be so quick to celebrate the stunning blue wave that washed over President Donald Trump this week.
American voters may have withdrawn the Republican mandate by giving Democrats the keys to Congress, but Trump can still direct his executive powers abroad, even as the opposition prepares to restrain him at home.
After a bruising midterm result for the U.S. president, a wounded Trump may seem like easy pickings for Chinese leader Xi Jinping , who will soon send negotiators to restart trade talks designed to neutralize America’s long-term tariff threat.
Xi had an understanding with Trump and knew what made him tick. But the political setback may make Trump much harder to predict .
Xi spent considerable resources on his rapprochement with Trump, including a state media campaign about Chinese resilience that stopped hostile economic acts by the United States and resulted in two glitzy state visits this year.
A promise to meet Trump at the APEC summit in southern China later this month, and again when Miami hosts the G20 meeting in December, has helped Xi build certainty into China’s relations with its top geopolitical rival.
Beijing may even go as far as to give Trump a foreign policy win at APEC by agreeing to a three-way meeting with Russia’s President Vladimir Putin in host city Shenzhen. Whether Xi makes any concrete commitments there is another question.
“Stability” has been the watchword in China for years, but it has extra weight this year after a campaign of purges swept up dozens of senior figures in elite Chinese politics and the military. Xi’s purges are about corruption in the Chinese Communist Party , but they’re also about loyalty—to him.
A recent gathering of the CCP’s Central Committee had the lowest attendance in over half a century, hinting at the scale of disciplinary action taken ahead of the party’s 21 st national congress in 12 months’ time, when Xi is widely expected to win an uncontested fourth 5-year term.
“Xi’s main political goal now is to secure another term at the 21st Party Congress. That requires not only a firm grip on power but also a case that his continued rule is legitimate and natural,” wrote Christopher Nye, a senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation think tank.
Xi used the latest gathering of party cadres “to resolve the problems of legitimacy created by the purge,” Nye wrote this week.
A fourth term could extend Xi’s rule over China to 20 years.
So, 2027 will be a delicate year for Xi. He’ll be wary of a Trump unleashed , who, despite being weakened domestically, could channel his energy into foreign policy matters, namely negotiations with China to extend or rip up the Busan truce that kept tariffs at a minimum in exchange for Chinese agricultural purchases and other key commitments.
“Beijing could conclude the election results mean Trump needs an economic agreement more than China does…. In that sense, Beijing could turn Trump’s political setback into a bargaining miscalculation that unsettles the very stability Xi is trying to preserve,” said Craig Singleton, senior director of the China program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank.
“If Beijing expects last night’s result to humble Trump, it is probably mistaken. He may have less room politically at home, but that could produce even bolder executive action abroad, including new pressure on Chinese companies, tighter economic-security measures and faster reshoring.
"Beijing should be careful about mistaking Trump’s political weakness for restraint in his China policy ."
Trump’s first presidency also began with personal diplomacy with China’s Xi before flattery gave way to full-blown systemic confrontation.
Trump hosted Xi at Mar-a-Lago in spring 2017 and Xi returned the favor in fall with a lavish state visit for Trump in Beijing. The two leaders appeared to agree on $250 billion in commercial deals, which later never materialized.
The trade war followed in 2018, along with the first stage of the tech war that targeted Chinese telecoms giant Huawei the following year. The Phase One trade deal in early 2020 eased tensions but didn’t stop them from boiling over once more during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Beijing was so concerned by the downturn in relations and the mixed signals out of the White House that it feared an “ October surprise ,” a military strike to rally support before Trump’s presidential race with Democrat Joe Biden.
Gen. Mark Milley, then chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, called his Chinese counterpart without Trump’s knowledge to assure him that the U.S. government was planning no such action—and to preempt any miscalculation by Beijing.
Trump’s last experience as a lame duck president didn’t lead to a hot war, but it locked in a new Cold War with China, one of economic decoupling and export controls. And on the last full day of the first Trump administration, his then secretary of state, Mike Pompeo, accused Xi’s government of genocide against Muslims in far-western China.
On the day Biden took office as the new U.S. president, China sanctioned former senior Trump officials in retaliation for the wild final weeks. The message to the new administration, and indeed the expectation, was that Trump’s hard-line China policies should be walked back. That didn’t happen and the rivalry was institutionalized.
Trump has no reason to hold back if Xi doesn’t play ball. And even with Trump neutered, the Democrats may not play nice.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan to close representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan to close representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan says it is closing its representative office in Papua New Guinea and will stop buying liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the country, blaming Chinese political pressure on the South Pacific nation.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday that Papua New Guinea had repeated previous demands that staff leave its office in the capital, Port Moresby, within a set deadline and had pushed for ⁠its closure.
These actions “reflect China’s continued use of political pressure and economic influence to interfere in other countries’ diplomatic decisions and suppress Taiwan’s international space”, it said in a statement.
China, which claims Taiwan as part of its territory, had welcomed Papua New Guinea’s decision in July to shutter Taiwan’s office in Port Moresby. Taipei rejected the move, and the office remained open in the interim.
The Pacific has long been an area for diplomatic competition between China and Taiwan. Papua New Guinea has formal diplomatic relations with China, but it had allowed Taiwan to have a representative office in Port Moresby.
Taiwan has formal diplomatic ties with only three Pacific Islands nations: Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands. It also has a representative office in Fiji. Just 12 countries maintain formal ⁠diplomatic ties with Taiwan.
Taiwan previously announced that it had stopped spot purchases of LNG from the South Pacific nation, but on Friday the ministry said it also would no longer sign new spot purchase contracts with the country.
Taiwanese LNG purchases accounted for one-third of Papua New Guinea’s exports.
Last year, Taiwan imported about 8 percent of its natural gas from Port Moresby.
Taipei will also end technical cooperation and assistance programmes, “including medical missions, related scholarship and talent development programmes”, the ministry said.
